name: Quien Sabe Glacier
approach: The Boston Basin approach starts at an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road roughly 21.5-23 miles from Marblemount (about 3,200-3,300 ft) - there's no formal trailhead sign, so watch your odometer. From the pullout, follow an old mining road/track for about a mile with minimal elevation gain, crossing Boston Creek. Watch closely for the unmaintained climbers' trail breaking off sharply to the right (cairns/flagging mark it, but it's easy to walk past); it climbs steeply through forest and a brushy old avalanche-slide path with sections of deadfall and loose footing. The path gains roughly 2,500 ft over about 2.5-3 miles to reach treeline and the lower Boston Basin camp (~5,300-5,400 ft), continuing to established upper camps around 6,200 ft. Plan on 3-4 hours trailhead to camp. Because this is a genuine climbers' path rather than a maintained trail, route-finding through the lower forest and slide-alder sections is the main approach hazard, and it can be greasy and slick when wet. Water is available from Boston Creek and seasonal snowmelt through mid-summer near camp. From high camp, rope up around 6,700 ft and make a rising traverse near the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower, picking a line up the Quien Sabe Glacier while avoiding crevasses - two common ascent lines (a left-side line and a more direct one) merge partway up. Expect to navigate a bergschrund via snow bridges around 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides in late season, before climbing to the Boston-Sahale col. From the col, a short but exposed snow traverse (crampons and axe recommended even late season) leads to the base of the summit block, finished with class 3-4 scrambling to the true summit.
descent: Most parties reverse the col traverse and Quien Sabe Glacier back down to Boston Basin camp, staying roped through the crevassed midsection and re-negotiating the two snow-bridge crossings near 8,100 ft and 7,600 ft. Coming off the true summit block itself typically involves one short rappel rather than a downclimb - commonly to the southeast/south off the summit block on tat/slings at a natural anchor, dropping onto easier class 3 terrain; a single 30m rope is generally sufficient for this short rappel, though confident parties without rope sometimes downclimb the class 3-4 moves in reverse instead. Some parties skip reversing the technical col/glacier terrain and instead continue down the south side into the Sahale Glacier basin (as on the standard Sahale Arm route), which involves a second, longer rappel - two 30m ropes, or a single 60m rope doubled, off tat anchors on the south face - down to a ledge, followed by a short 3rd-class downscramble to the Sahale Glacier, then a hike out via the Sahale Arm/Cascade Pass Trail. Either way, expect real crevasse hazard on the glacier descent that increases through the season, plus loose, chossy rock on the south-side downscramble option.
hazards: Numerous crevasses and exposed blue ice on the Quien Sabe Glacier, worse late in the season
Rockfall off the Sharkfin Tower face, especially with multiple parties on route
Loose rock on the final summit scramble
Exposed, unprotected snow traverse across the col
Route-finding on the unmaintained Boston Basin climbers' trail
Significant bear activity in Boston Basin — food storage required

waysIn.name: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
hazards: Missing the sharp right turn off the mine roadbed onto the climbers' trail
Bergschrund at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, open both sides late season
Rockfall from the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower during the rising traverse
Exposed rock-and-snow ridge above the col, corniced into early summer
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer

name: Sahale Arm / Sahale Glacier
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the Cascade Pass Trail through old-growth timber via roughly 35 well-graded switchbacks, gaining about 1,800 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases through subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.5-3.7 miles. At the pass, take the left (north) fork signed for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open, increasingly rocky ridge crest - the Sahale Arm Trail, about 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft of additional gain, with views down to Doubtful Lake (a worthwhile ~1-mile, 1,000-ft side trip on a signed spur if you want water or to scout the basin) and across to Johannesburg Mountain, Magic Mountain, and Mixup Peak. The maintained trail ends around 7,200-7,600 ft at Sahale Glacier Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads that also serves as the NPS-permitted high camp (wilderness permit required, quota-limited in summer). Total trailhead-to-camp distance is about 6 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain, typically 4-5 hours. Above camp, rope up for glacier travel - the Sahale Glacier is small and generally low crevasse hazard compared to nearby glaciers but should not be crossed unroped without current beta, especially late season - and ascend directly to the southwest base of the summit pyramid. From there a short, exposed stretch of steep snow and 3rd-4th class rock leads to a ledge just below the true summit, finished by a short, awkward chimney-like move (about 5.0) onto the summit block. Water is reliably found at Doubtful Lake and from snowmelt/tarns near Sahale Glacier Camp early-to-mid season, but sources can dry up by late summer, so carry enough for the switchback climb to the pass.
descent: Below Sahale Glacier Camp, descent is simply a reverse of the Sahale Arm and Cascade Pass trails back to the trailhead. Getting off the summit block itself is usually done by rappel, though some parties downclimb it instead, often with a belay through the crux. Parties commonly rappel the south side, where the rock strata slopes away from the face and is comparatively free of loose blocks, off a well-used natural anchor - typically a cluster of several slings (often faded/sun-worn and worth backing up) wrapped around a large boulder, sometimes with rap rings added. With a 60m rope doubled (about 30m of rope per strand), most parties reach easier ground or a second station in a single rappel; with a 30m single line or 50m doubled, expect an awkward down-scramble to bridge the remaining gap, and some parties instead break it into two shorter rappels. From the base of the rappel, a short 3rd-class scramble/downclimb regains the top of the Sahale Glacier, which is then recrossed roped back to camp. No unusual descent hazards beyond the rappel itself and standard glacier crevasse hazard, which increases as the season progresses and the glacier opens up.
hazards: Crevasses on the Sahale Glacier, especially exposed and icy by late summer
Steep snow on the approach that can require an ice axe into July
Loose rock and exposure on the final 3rd/4th-class summit scramble
Fast-changing alpine weather with little shelter above Cascade Pass
Significant bear activity around camps — food storage required

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake

waysIn.name: Car-to-car day push
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, long daylight
waysIn.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you could not get a permit for Sahale Glacier Camp, or want to skip the quota; a strong party can do it in one long day, carrying glacier gear the whole way.

name: South Slopes via Emerald-Saska Col
approach: Standard access is the North Fork Entiat River Trail (#1437) from the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (el. ~3,940 ft, at the end of Forest Road 5606, about 35.3 mi from the town of Entiat via Entiat River Road/Forest Road 51 then FR 5606). The trail crosses old fire-damaged forest with blowdown for its first miles, enters Glacier Peak Wilderness at about mile 4 (free self-issue wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead kiosk), and reaches the Pyramid Creek/Fern Lake trail junction roughly 7-9 miles in depending on trip reports and current trailhead access (road washouts have periodically forced parties to start several miles below the official trailhead — check current Forest Service alerts). From the junction, the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail climbs west about 1,000 ft over roughly 1-1.5 miles into the high basin between Emerald and Saska; most parties camp either at Fox Camp near the junction or push on to a larch-meadow camp directly beneath the Emerald-Saska col for a shorter summit day. In early September the basin below the col has a camp with running water and dense larches; scree on the way down is fast to boot-ski.
descent: Descend the same col traverse and basin scree. In early-to-mid season, continuous snow below the col allows a glissade or boot-ski descent; by August-September this becomes loose scree and dirt requiring slow, controlled steps rather than good scree-skiing. Stay well clear of the cliff bands below the southwest face when snow-covered or icy — a documented February 2020 winter-ascent party lost a ski over these cliffs after misjudging the descent line in icy conditions.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and summit ridge — helmet recommended
Lingering snow/ice in the col and summit gullies into early-mid July in heavy snow years, with avalanche potential on the southwest face in winter/spring
Cliff bands below the southwest face have caught descending parties off guard in icy or snow-covered conditions
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage

waysIn.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
waysIn.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
waysIn.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead at about 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
hazards: Heavy blowdown and washouts on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past fires and storms; hot, shadeless valley bottom
Primitive upper Pyramid Creek trail leads to the high basin camp
Loose rock and rockfall in the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge; helmet advised
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July
Cliff bands below the south-west face have caught descending parties in icy or snowy conditions
Narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest to be avoided rather than followed

waysIn.name: Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass
waysIn.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then climb the trail past the Domke Lake junction and up Emerald Park Creek to Emerald Park, about 6.5 miles, and on another two miles to Milham Pass. Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska and pick up the south-slopes route there. A long, remote approach that suits parties already on the Lake Chelan side.
hazards: Boat access up Lake Chelan, then a long, remote approach of about 6.5 miles to Emerald Park and two more to Milham Pass
Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska; route-finding needed
Loose rock and rockfall in the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge; helmet advised
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July
Cliff bands below the south-west face have caught descending parties in icy or snowy conditions
Narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest to be avoided rather than followed
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you are already on the Lake Chelan side with a boat ride to Lucerne; a long remote approach over Milham Pass instead of the North Fork Entiat road.

name: Scarface
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), follow the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles, bearing left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, finishing with a boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Top off water here. Head toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, watch for wet snow into July), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully system. Scarface climbs the gully just left of the West Face route's start; this terrain is very loose and exposed, so extra care with rope-up/spacing is warranted through the final approach scramble. Total trailhead-to-base time runs about 3.5-4 hours, in line with neighboring routes.
descent: Scarface tops out near the other West Face-area routes and shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block (avoiding the balanced boulder) down to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base (45 min-1hr). A short section near the top is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) instead of downclimbing. No full rappel of the route itself is required under normal conditions.
hazards: significant loose rock and rockfall danger, especially on lower pitches — coordinate belays and protection removal carefully to avoid dropping debris on partners below

name: Scramble Route
approach: The Eagle Peak Trailhead is about 300 feet past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River. From there, a maintained trail (about 7.2 miles round trip, ~2,955 ft gain) climbs steeply through forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky terrain for a final half mile to the 5,700-foot Eagle Peak Saddle, where the maintained trail ends. The saddle is exposed with cliff edges that can be corniced with lingering snow into June; routes onto Eagle Peak itself continue past the saddle as a scramble.
descent: The descent from the summit to the saddle involves reversing the Class 3 scramble, with the crux rock step being slightly more difficult going down. Best technique is to face outward, pivot right to face into the rock wall, then step down with a blind foothold. Use 'veggie-belay' (roots and branches) as needed for security. Once back at the saddle, descend the well-graded trail switchbacks through alpine meadow (watch for exposure and uneven terrain in the saddle area—use extreme caution as falls could be deadly), then through old-growth forest. Stream crossing and gradual descent continues to the Nisqually Suspension Bridge and trailhead parking.
hazards: Avalanche danger on steep meadow in winter (requires avalanche skills)
Rockfall hazard when multiple parties on route
Wet conditions increase scrambling difficulty

waysIn.name: Longmire, the Nisqually suspension bridge and the Eagle Peak Trail to the saddle
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the saddle can be corniced with lingering snow into June
waysIn.notes:
The Eagle Peak trailhead is about 300 ft past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River at Longmire, which is normally reachable year-round.

The maintained trail — about 7.2 miles round trip and nearly 3,000 ft of gain — climbs steeply through old-growth forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky ground for a final half mile to Eagle Peak Saddle at about 5,700-5,720 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

The saddle is exposed, with cliff edges that hold cornices into early summer. Everything above it is scrambling on a climbers' path.
hazards: Exposed terrain at the saddle with cliff edges and cornices into June — falls here are fatal
Loose holds on the class 4 rock step, which most parties should bypass
The crux step is harder to descend than to climb, with a blind foothold
Rockfall between parties on a narrow ridge
Steep meadow avalanche terrain in winter
Wet rock materially increases the scrambling difficulty

name: Standard Route
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road (paved/gravel Forest Road 15, inside North Cascades NP boundary — verify current road/washout status at nps.gov/noca before driving). Take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain up open switchbacks and through Basin Creek/Doubtful Lake side-valley scenery to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last reliable trail tread and a good water stop. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country south on a boot path, climbing the Cache Glacier snowfield (permanent snow into late season; crampons and axe recommended) to Cache Col (~6,900 ft). The col's far (south) lip commonly corniced through mid-summer — this is a real hazard on both the ascent and the descent back over it. Drop steeply off the south side of Cache Col to the Kool-Aid Lake basin (established camps, reliable water). From Kool-Aid Lake, contour east around the toe of the Cache Glacier and climb to the 'Red Ledge,' a narrow, exposed rock ledge running beneath Art's Knoll that is the standard (least-technical) way through a cliff band and is considered one of the route-finding/exposure cruxes of the whole approach; in low-snow years the alternate Middle Cascade Glacier line can bypass it. Past Red Ledge, traverse to Yang Yang Lakes (~6,300 ft, good camping and water — most parties treat this or Kool-Aid Lake as their overnight base). From Yang Yang Lakes, ascend the broad Le Conte Glacier — a genuine crevassed glacier requiring roped travel — to the Le Conte-Sentinel Col (~7,300 ft), a flat notch atop the glacier with dry bivy sites and the jump-off point for the peak itself. From the col, easy scrambling leads onto snow filling the basin against Sentinel's west face; climb increasingly steep snow (can exceed 35-40°, crampons/axe useful) to its top, then follow an obvious ledge leftward (north) across the face past a short cliff band, then turn straight up steep, gravelly/scree terrain to a short step of upper-class-3/low-class-5 climbing, finishing with roughly 600 ft up the broad west ridge to the summit. Given the ~45 km round trip and glacier travel, this is realistically a multi-day trip (camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Yang Yang Lakes) rather than a car-to-car day climb for most parties.
descent: Descend the same line used on the ascent — the west ridge and the leftward-slanting face ledge — rather than the looser, steeper east ridge, which is explicitly warned against. Downclimb the short upper-class-3/low-class-5 step facing in, then descend the gravel/scree below it, pick up the diagonal ledge back rightward onto the west-face snowfield, and face-in downclimb or plunge-step the steep snow back down to the Le Conte-Sentinel Col. From there, reverse the approach: rope up again for the Le Conte Glacier's crevasses down to Yang Yang Lakes, back across the exposed Red Ledge, over Cache Col (cornice hazard on the descent to Kool-Aid Lake side just as on the ascent), and down the Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. No fixed or bolted rappel exists on Sentinel's standard route — it is a scramble walk-off/downclimb of the ascent line. Some parties place an optional single-rope hand-line or short rappel off a sling/picket to protect the low-5th-class step or the steepest snow near the col in early-season or wet conditions, but this is situational, not a required or documented feature of the route, so treat any rappel as optional protection rather than a mandatory technical descent.
hazards: Crevasses on the Le Conte Glacier — rope up for glacier travel
Cornices near Cache Col and along the approach ridgelines, worst in early season (June-early July)
Short low-5th-class rock step above the 7,400 ft snow ramp on the west ridge — can be wet/icy
The Red Ledge traverse between Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake is exposed when banked with steep snow
Whiteout/poor-visibility route-finding across the glaciated approach basins
Extreme remoteness — no cell coverage, long self-rescue times

waysIn.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
waysIn.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
hazards: Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed; rope up and carry a rescue kit
Red Ledge is serious when banked with snow, common into early July
Cornices near Cache Col and approach ridgelines, worst in early season
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times

waysIn.name: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse
waysIn.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, walk the Downey Creek trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge, then cross the Dana Glacier country to White Rock Lakes. From the lakes, work back up onto the South Cascade Glacier to reach the peak. Plan on several days of off-trail and glacier travel.
hazards: Several days of off-trail and glacier travel from Downey Creek via the brushy Bachelor Creek path, Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge
Crevasses on the Dana and South Cascade Glaciers
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times
waysIn.whyThisWay: When working the Ptarmigan Traverse from the south end, or linking Sentinel into it, after a long walk up Downey Creek and several days of off-trail and glacier travel.

name: Southwest Slopes
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, end of FR 6211 off Chiwawa River Road), start on Phelps Creek Trail #1511. At about a quarter mile the Carne Mountain Trail splits off steeply to the right (skip it); stay on Phelps Creek Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the creek. At 2.6 mi you cross into Glacier Peak Wilderness. Continue to roughly 3.4–3.5 mi, where the trail crosses Leroy Creek (about 4,140 ft) on a log/rock crossing that can run high with snowmelt in early summer — this is the key junction. Immediately after the crossing, leave the maintained trail and turn right (northeast) onto the unmaintained Leroy Creek climbers' trail, which follows the north side of Leroy Creek and gains roughly 2,000 ft in about 1.5 miles of steep, sometimes brushy, boot-track tread — this is the stiffest sustained pitch of the day. It tops out in the open meadows/talus of Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft, a common camp spot with reliable water from Leroy Creek and views of Seven Fingered Jack, Mount Maude, and Ice Lakes basin above. From camp, aim for the broad southwest slope of the peak: two parallel lines lead out of the basin — a rock gully straight up to the lower southwest slope, or a gentler ridge to its right — and they merge in a flat spot around 6,700–6,800 ft where the wide, rocky southwest slope proper begins (some parties climb to the base of cliffs near 7,200 ft then cut right to the 7,800 ft bench, which is described as the easiest line). From there it's an extended ascent of loose talus and scree — boulder-hop and pick the cleanest line, favoring rock over scree where possible — trending slightly left up the slope toward the summit rocks, with a few short steeper steps that can be passed on either side without real difficulty. Near the top, cross a shallow ravine below the summit spires and follow a faint climbers' trail up to the left-most (true) summit block at 9,078 ft. Hazards are loose talus/scree underfoot the entire upper mountain, exposed ridge/slope travel above treeline with no shelter from weather, and route-finding that gets harder in poor visibility since there is no single defined trail above Leroy Basin; a lingering snow gully in the entry couloir in early season may require an ice axe. Basin-to-summit is commonly quoted at about 3 hours in good conditions; round trip is roughly 13 miles with 5,600 ft of gain.
descent: Descend the ascent line in reverse: down the southwest scree/talus slope to the flat spot at about 6,700–6,800 ft, then drop back into Leroy Basin via whichever of the rock-gully or ridge lines you prefer (the ridge line is generally more stable underfoot than the loose gully). This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard Southwest Slopes route, so rappels = 0. From Leroy Basin, retrace the steep climbers' trail down along Leroy Creek back to the Phelps Creek Trail junction (roughly 2,000 ft of descent in 1.5 miles on loose, sometimes braided boot-tread — easy to lose the tread on the way down, especially in the lower brushy section), then follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 back out to the trailhead. Watch for: loose, ball-bearing scree on the upper mountain that makes for slow, careful downclimbing and real rockfall risk onto parties below (stay bunched or well-spaced, avoid stacking climbers directly below each other in the gully); lingering steep snow in the entry couloir/gully in early-to-mid season, which some parties glissade but which has rock runout hazard lower down; and the general difficulty of route-finding the correct braid of the Leroy Creek climbers' trail in the timber below the basin, particularly at dusk or in poor visibility. No technical rope work is required for this route in typical summer conditions.
hazards: High, cold Leroy Creek ford just below Leroy Basin — often the technical crux of the trip, especially before August
Loose scree and rockfall on the southwest slope, worsened when parties climb above or below one another
A narrow, deep ravine near the summit spires that can hold snow/ice well into summer
Route-finding through the jagged summit 'fingers' to reach the true (leftmost) high point
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on the exposed upper slope in summer
Steep snow in the entry gully out of Leroy Basin in early season, with avalanche potential on the approach slopes

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek to Leroy Basin, then the couloir toward the Maude col
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; a snow gully out of the basin may want an ice axe early in the season
waysIn.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead at about 3,500 ft, walk the Phelps Creek trail roughly three and a half miles to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft. It is occasionally given as two and a half miles, but three and a half is the usual figure. Immediately after the crossing, turn right onto the unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek. It gains roughly two thousand feet in about a mile and a half of steep, sometimes brushy boot tread and is the hardest sustained work of the day. It levels into the flat Leroy Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, which is the standard camp, with reliable water. Round trip for the peak is commonly given as about thirteen miles with 5,600 ft of gain, a figure two independent parties record.
hazards: Uniformly loose rock and scree on the whole upper mountain — this group has a bad reputation and deserves it
Party-inflicted rockfall in the couloir out of the basin; small parties are strongly preferable
A lingering snow gully in the entry couloir early season
No shelter above the basin and no defined trail, so poor visibility makes the spires-and-ravine sequence much harder
Steep, brushy climbers' trail gaining two thousand feet out of the valley

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: From the Boston Basin climbers' trailhead on Cascade River Road (~3,200–3,400 ft, ~21.7 mi from Marblemount; the upper road is prone to washouts, so check its status), pick up the unmaintained but well-worn Boston Basin climbers' path. It switchbacks steeply up through forest on old roadbed/boot path, crosses a couple of small streams (last reliable water before camp), and breaks out of the trees onto open meadow slabs. Expect roughly 3.2 mi and 2,500 ft of gain to the designated low camp (~5,300–5,700 ft), about 2.5–3 hours for a laden party; the high camp sits higher still on a meadow knoll around 6,300–6,400 ft and shaves real time off the summit day. From camp, contour/ascend slabs and easy snowfields on the left (climber's) side of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Sharkfin Col, rope up for glacier travel, and traverse east along the top of the glacier for several hundred feet until you're directly beneath the tower's obvious approach gully. This gully runs 35° snow in early season and degrades to loose class 2–3 scree/rubble by late summer; crampons and an axe (or trekking poles once it's melted out) help. Follow it up to a notch/terrace at the base of the southeast ridge proper. Route-finding here is the crux of the approach and has real consequences: a fatal 2005 accident on this peak began when a party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully next to the standard line, so confirm you're in the correct gully (directly below the ridge, not an adjacent chute) before committing, and be alert for rockfall from parties above in this popular, loose corridor.
descent: Descend by reversing the ridge: downclimb the upper class 4 crest a short distance (commonly cited as roughly 20 ft) to a chockstone/horn or fixed tat-and-ring station near the top of the gully, then rappel and downclimb the rest of the way back to the glacier along essentially the same line you climbed. Trip reports converge on roughly 4–5 rappels total to get from the ridge back down through the gully to the Quien Sabe Glacier — a short rappel or two off the upper ridge to regain the notch/gully, followed by two or three longer rappels down the couloir itself (some parties do the gully in two long raps of ~30 m each using two ropes tied together or doubled, others break it into shorter 15–20 m pitches on natural anchors). A single 60 m rope is generally enough for any individual station, and doubling/joining two ropes lets you skip stations in the gully if you're moving as a pair. Anchors are a mix of fixed tat-and-ring stations left by prior parties, slung chockstones and horns, and at least one station reported built from a couple of old pitons — quality is inconsistent and should not be trusted blindly. This matters here specifically: a well-documented 2005 accident on this exact descent involved a single-point natural anchor (one cordelette/webbing around a loose block, no backup) that failed under a multi-person rappel and resulted in three fatalities. Back up marginal anchors, rappel one at a time where anchors are questionable, and expect loose/blocky rock and, in shoulder season, wet rope and snow/ice in the gully. Once back on the Quien Sabe Glacier, downclimb/walk the snowfields back to camp, reversing the approach.
hazards: Rappel/anchor failure — a July 2005 accident here killed 3 climbers when an overloaded, unbacked anchor failed roughly 10 ft into a rappel
Rockfall and loose rock in the approach gully, worse as seasonal snow melts out to scree
Route-finding error into the wrong gully, a contributing factor in the 2005 accident
Afternoon thunderstorms typical of North Cascades summers

waysIn.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
waysIn.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
waysIn.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.
hazards: Wrong-gully error — the defining hazard of this approach, with a fatal precedent
Bergschrund or seracs barring the direct gully entry
Rockfall in the gully, natural and from parties above
Poor natural anchors — a boulder anchor failure caused the 2005 fatalities
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe traverse

waysIn.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
waysIn.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
waysIn.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.
hazards: Wrong-gully error, harder to rule out once the snow has gone
Loose scree and climber-triggered rockfall in the gully
Open moat at the glacier-rock junction
Rockfall from parties rappelling the descent line
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late season, August to September, once the approach gully has melted out to loose scree; expect rockfall risk from parties above and a moat at the glacier edge.

name: Crater Rim Scramble (from Easton Glacier)
approach: Start at the Park Butte Trailhead (elev. ~3,360 ft) at the end of Forest Service Road 13, reached via the Baker Lake Highway/Sulfur Creek Road turnoff (do not repeat the drive-in here — this covers the hike only). From the trailhead register, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. The trail crosses Sulfur Creek on a footbridge just past the trailhead; at about 0.7 mile it crosses Rocky Creek — braided, silty glacial melt in a boulder field that can run high and fast on warm afternoons, usually bridged by a seasonal footbridge from about July. Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche-path terrain, crosses a couple of additional meltwater streams, then switchbacks up a forested slope into Morovitz Meadows (~2 miles in). Near the meadow, stay left at the signed junction with the Scott Paul Trail #603.1 (which splits right) to stay on Park Butte Trail, then take the next right fork onto the Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass/the glacier (straight ahead leads to the Park Butte lookout instead). Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 climbs onto the crest of a narrow lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a distinctive, uniformly graded ridge (hence the name) with exposed, steep drop-offs on both sides in places; use care in wind or on icy/frosty mornings. Designated Railroad Grade camps sit at 2.25–2.75 miles from the trailhead; High Camp sites are at about 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp, at roughly 5,900 ft, marks the end of maintained tread. From Sandy Camp the route continues cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier, typically 3–4 hours car-to-camp for most parties. Rope up for glacier travel around 6,800–7,200 ft (conditions-dependent) and ascend the Easton Glacier heading north toward the Sherman Crater rim; the standard line stays east (climber's right) of the glacier's major crevasse bands, though route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the approach and shifts season to season — wanding the route is standard practice given frequent whiteout/cloud cap conditions on Baker's south side. Above roughly 9,600–9,800 ft the route skirts the rim of Sherman Crater, where active fumaroles vent sulfurous steam (occasionally noticeable by smell and visible venting) — stay on the established boot path here and keep gear away from the acidic, degraded rock near the vents. No potable water exists at the trailhead itself; plan on treating water from Sulfur/Rocky Creek near the start or from snowmelt at High/Sandy Camp. In late June the Park Butte trail is snow-free low down; snow begins at the top of the switchbacks and camps near 5,400 ft are often full, so many go on to about 6,000 ft.
descent: This is a glacier walk-up/scramble with no fixed rappel stations anywhere on the standard line — descent is a walk-off, reversing the ascent route. From the Sherman Peak/crater-rim high point, downclimb the summit snow slope and the West Ridge back to the crater rim first — most parties find this the psychologically hardest part of the day simply because of the steep snow right below the summit; face-in plunge-stepping or a careful glissade (only when runout and snow conditions are safe, and never near crevasses or the crater's exposed rock) is typical. Continue back down through the Sherman Crater rim area, staying alert for the same fumarole/loose-rock hazard noted on the approach, then re-rope for the descent back through the Easton Glacier's crevasse field, following your ascent wands/tracks rather than freelancing a new line, since crevasse bridges can fail or shift through the day. Below the glacier's toe, pick up the Railroad Grade moraine-crest trail back to Sandy/High Camp and down through Morovitz Meadows to the Park Butte Trailhead, re-crossing Rocky Creek near the end. In good visibility this is a straightforward reverse of the route; in Baker's characteristic cloud cap or whiteout conditions, GPS/wands become essential since the moraine crest and crater rim offer little natural handrail. There is no roped rappelling on this route in normal conditions. Early-afternoon June descents sink thigh-deep in warm soft snow; start the return from the summit early.
hazards: Sulfurous volcanic gas (SO2/H2S) venting from Sherman Crater fumaroles — corrosive to skin, eyes, and gear; avoid lingering downwind of active vents
Crevasses on the Easton/Squak Glaciers, worse in low-snow late-season conditions
Loose, acid-altered volcanic rock on and near the crater rim
Sudden whiteout/lenticular cloud buildup typical of an isolated, wind-exposed volcano
Historic lahar hazard from potential crater-wall collapse — actively monitored by USGS/MBVRC, currently assessed as low near-term risk

waysIn.name: Park Butte Trail and the Railroad Grade moraine to Sandy Camp, then the Easton Glacier to the crater rim
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of FR-13 near 3,360 ft, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. The trail crosses Sulfur Creek on a footbridge just past the trailhead; at about 0.7 mile it crosses Rocky Creek — braided, silty glacial melt in a boulder field that runs high and fast on warm afternoons, usually bridged by a seasonal footbridge from about July.

Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche terrain, crosses more meltwater streams, and switchbacks into Morovitz Meadows about two miles in. Near the meadow stay left at the signed Scott Paul Trail #603.1 junction to stay on Park Butte, then take the next right onto Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass. Straight ahead at that second fork goes to the Park Butte lookout instead — a pleasant hike and the wrong one.

Railroad Grade #603.2 climbs onto the crest of the lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a uniformly graded ridge, hence the name, with steep drops on both sides in places. Designated camps sit at 2.25-2.75 miles; High Camp is around 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft is where maintained tread ends.

There is no potable water at the trailhead. Treat from Sulfur or Rocky Creek near the start, or melt at camp.
hazards: The braided glacial crossing of Rocky Creek, which runs high on warm afternoons
Exposed drops on both sides of the Railroad Grade moraine crest, worse in wind or on frosty mornings
A crevasse field that is the technical crux of the approach and moves season to season
Baker's characteristic cloud cap and whiteouts on the south side, above the last natural handrail
Active fumaroles and acid-degraded rock at the Sherman Crater rim

name: Standard Route
approach: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.
descent: From the top of the balanced rock, most parties do not reverse the shoulder-stand/friction sequence (considered the route's real crux to downclimb) and instead rappel a single fixed bolt/chain anchor at the summit straight back down to the belay ledge - a short (~20 ft) single-strand rappel that any rope length easily covers. From the ledge, downclimb or step off to the talus/blocks at the base of the pillar. From there, descent is a reversal of the approach: regain the ridge crest and drop back toward Table Rock and the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, picking down through the boulder field and the Class 2-3 gully system - loose, rockfall-prone terrain where a helmet is strongly advised, and where parties note the unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself, especially near dusk. Regain the climbers' boot path at the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back up and over Longs Pass to return to the trailhead. This is a single-pitch feature, so no multi-rappel sequence is needed for the balanced rock itself - the one bolted rappel off the top is the only roped descent on the Standard Route; parties climbing the broader Sherpa Peak West Ridge to reach the main summit (a separate, longer route) report needing several additional rappels off that ridge, but that is not part of this Standard Route's descent.
hazards: Loose rock on the approach gully and along the ridge traverse to the block
Old fixed ring piton and rappel bolt of unknown age/condition — do not trust blindly, back up with your own gear
Unprotected, exposed shoulder-stand/friction start — a fall before protection is reached could be serious
Unmaintained, easy-to-lose climbers' path on the north approach (blowdowns, faint cairns)
Afternoon thunderstorms common over the Stuart Range in summer

waysIn.name: Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the gully system above Ingalls Creek is dry
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda / Longs Pass trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take Longs Pass Trail #1229 through open pine and sage switchbacks about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft.

Drop off the north side on the steep eroded boot path, losing 1,400-1,600 ft over about a mile to Ingalls Creek at roughly 4,800 ft. Ford the creek — a rock-hop in low water, a real wet crossing in snowmelt — and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail east about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike junction at about 4,700 ft. That junction is the last dependable water before the alpine basin.

A climbers' boot path switchbacks up through forest and talus from there; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide between two gullies and drop into the eastern one, which leads toward Sherpa. Class 2 slopes above it reach Table Rock, a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and the usual high bivy.

Carry all your water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction; the upper basin is dry.
hazards: A steep, loose descent off Longs Pass in both directions
An Ingalls Creek ford that is a genuine crossing in early-season snowmelt
Loose rockfall-prone gully and basin terrain — helmets strongly advised
A dry upper basin: no water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction
An exposed Class 3-4 crest traverse to reach the pillar
A single ageing bolt as the rappel anchor off the top
The unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself

name: Sherpa Glacier
approach: From the Lake Stuart Trailhead, hike the Lake Stuart-Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599); at about 2.2 miles a fork splits toward Colchuck Lake (left) and Lake Stuart (right) — leave the maintained trail near the meadow around 4,500 ft and head southwest, following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream. After a couple of miles, climb a steep talus/boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa/Stuart Glaciers. Sherpa Glacier climbers ascend directly from this basin; Stuart Glacier Couloir climbers continue up into the couloir on Stuart's north side from the same basin. This is the standard approach for a compact two-day outing on these routes, though it can alternatively be reached from the south via Goat Pass by traversing across the upper Stuart Glacier.
descent: Early in the season the Sherpa Glacier itself is the best way down: reverse the roughly 40-degree snow of the couloir, facing in, back to the camp in the basin at its foot. When the snow is hard and icy this becomes a no-fall descent that may need rappels to reach the glacier safely, so carry pickets or other anchors and rope. Later in the summer, or if you are leaving the basin for the south side, continue over the summit and down the Cascadian Couloir to Ingalls Creek and Longs Pass; that way is loose scree and talus and sheds rock onto anyone below.
hazards: A real bergschrund forms at the top of the glacier before the couloir; late-season ascents face broken glacial snow and may need extra rappel gear as the glacier degrades through summer

waysIn.name: Mountaineer Creek south fork to the basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Jul while the glacier still carries continuous snow; it is also the standard early-season descent off the north side, which is when most parties are on it
waysIn.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the Lake Stuart / Colchuck Lake trail past the fork and leave the maintained tread near the meadow at about 4,500 ft, heading southwest and following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream.

After a couple of miles a steep talus and boulder slope leads into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak. This is the standard camp for the whole north side, and the flat ground itself is the arrival cue.

The glacier has three parts and it is worth knowing them before you set off in the dark: a lower snowfield, the glacier proper, and a steeper couloir in its northwest corner. Parties rope for the short glacier section and take the rope off above it.

This is a compact two-day outing, and it is the line most parties descend after climbing the Ice Cliff Glacier — so if you meet people coming down it at midday they are probably finishing a different climb.
hazards: Crevasses in the middle section of the glacier and an icefall at its toe
Wet-snow avalanche and rockfall onto the glacier as the day warms
Straying right into the Ice Cliff Glacier's serac fall zone in poor visibility
A steep, unmaintained talus climb into the hanging valley with no trail
Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that move with the snowpack

name: West Ridge
approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/FS-9737, ~4,300 ft), take the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) roughly 2.3 miles and about 2,300 ft of gain to Longs Pass (~6,200 ft), a broad open saddle. From the pass, drop steeply down the north side (a boot path, with snow fingers usable for glissading in early season) about 1,300-1,400 ft to the Ingalls Creek drainage (~4,800 ft). Ford or rock-hop Ingalls Creek (can run high with early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it right (east) about a half to full mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction. Leave the maintained trail here for a boot/climbers' path (sometimes called the "tapeworm trail") that switchbacks up through timber and brush before opening into meadow beneath Sherpa and Argonaut Peaks. Gain the rounded rib dividing the Cascadian Couloir drainage from the basin under Sherpa, then contour around 5,800 ft into the snow-holding basin below the West Ridge; kick steps up final snow/talus slopes to a common bivy/base-camp shelf around 7,400 ft (a flat table-rock area) or continue straight to the ridge base. Total gain from the car to the base of technical climbing runs roughly 3,400-4,700 ft depending on whether you camp or go car-to-car, with 6-7 hours of hiking typical for the one-way approach. Water is available at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season; the brushy bushwhack down to Ingalls Creek and the long boulder/talus field beneath Sherpa are the main route-finding and stamina cruxes of the approach.
descent: The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy bundle of slings wrapped around a few small loose rocks next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. Total rappel count is commonly described as four stations (two singles, a scramble, one more single, then one double-rope rappel); some parties count this as three rappels depending on how stations are combined, so expect 3-4 total.
hazards: Rockfall on the approach traverse around 5,800 ft
Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August on the exposed ridge crest
Loose blocks on the summit ridge near the Balanced Rock

waysIn.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and up from Ingalls Creek
waysIn.season: mid-Jul-Sep; snow lingers on the approach benches and north-facing ground into early July
waysIn.notes:
Esmeralda Basin / Longs Pass Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FS-9737), about 4,300 ft. Longs Pass Trail (#1229) for roughly 2.3 miles and 2,300 ft to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft.

Drop the north side, losing 1,300-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft — early season there are snow fingers here that glissade well. Ford or rock-hop the creek, join the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it right (east) about a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at about 4,700 ft.

Leave the maintained trail there. Ascend rightward across the meadow to where the slope steepens at about 5,000 ft, cross the stream, and climb the rib staying left of its crest. At around 5,800 ft traverse right, cross over the rib, and contour into the basin below Sherpa.

There is a flat table-rock shelf at about 7,400 ft that parties use as a bivy or gear-up spot. Around 6,000 ft the climbers' path enters a spot where the gully narrows; from there some parties gain a few hundred feet east to the divide separating that gully from the one leading more directly toward Sherpa, then drop grudgingly into the correct gully and take class 2 slopes up to the table rock.

Six to seven hours one way is typical. Water at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season.
hazards: Steep loose drop off the north side of Longs Pass
Ingalls Creek ford runs high in early-season melt
Brushy bushwhack between the Ingalls Creek Trail and the open basin
Long boulder and talus field beneath Sherpa — a stamina and route-finding crux both
Picking the correct gully out of the basin: the obvious narrowing at ~6,000 ft is a decision point, not the line
Descent is rappels off mixed fixed slings, some reported as poor — carry cord

name: Silver Star Glacier
approach: Park at the broad pullout/overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165–166 (about 4 miles east of Washington Pass), where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain. From the pullout, drop down the embankment roughly 150–200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log (logjams shift year to year — scout up- and downstream for the best crossing, and be ready to ford in high water/early season, when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt). On the far bank, pick up the unofficial but well-defined climber's trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From here the trail climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500–3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting creek-side water access early on — treat the crossing at Early Winters Creek as your last reliable water until camp. At around 6,000–6,400 ft the grade eases at 'the Bench,' an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby; this is the standard overnight camp for a two-day trip and a natural break point/turnaround check for day-trippers. Above the bench, continue up open subalpine terrain toward Burgundy Col. Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col — it is loose and exposed; instead stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col itself (roughly 7,800 ft). Total gain from the highway to the col is on the order of 3,500–4,400 ft depending on exact trailhead/camp used. Hazards on the approach: the Early Winters Creek crossing (cold, log can be wet/mossy or washed out), steep eroding/brushy tread that's easy to lose in the timber, and loose rock ('kitty litter') on the final gully/traverse into the col.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent route. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3–4 rock (the same easy, somewhat exposed ledge system used on the way up) back to the col between the east and west summits; several trip reports and topo photos document a natural/slung rappel anchor near the true summit that parties use to bypass the most exposed section of this downclimb — a single rappel with one 50 m rope (or a 60 m rope doubled) is enough to get below the crux and onto easier ground, though plenty of parties simply downclimb the whole way and skip it entirely, so treat this as an optional, not mandatory, rappel with a natural anchor (sling on a horn/block), not bolts. From the base of the summit scramble, work back down onto the Silver Star Glacier and re-descend it, wrapping below the rock slabs of Burgundy Spire; note that this traverse dips below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so you must reclimb a couple hundred feet of steep snow from the low point back up to the col — a sting in the tail that catches parties expecting a pure descent. From Burgundy Col, downclimb the steep snow and loose, unstable 'kitty litter' rock/gully back toward the bench; this section is notoriously slow and has taken parties 3+ hours in reported descents. From the bench, follow the climber's trail back down through the timber to Early Winters Creek, re-cross (log or ford), and climb the short embankment back up to the SR-20 pullout. A less common alternative is to descend the east side via the Silver Star Creek basin instead of reversing to Burgundy Col (avoiding the reclimb to the col), but this exits at a different highway pullout and requires a car shuttle or road walk back, so most parties simply reverse the ascent.
hazards: Crevasses opening on the upper glacier later in the season
Loose, sandy scree in the gully below Burgundy Col
Exposed, unroped 4th-to-low-5th-class moves on the final summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms and softening snow on the descent
Wildfire deadfall and unstable burned slopes on the Silver Star Creek approach

waysIn.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more

waysIn.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you would rather not do the whole climb in one long day: camp at the bench, cross the glacier on firm morning snow, and be back over the col before afternoon softening.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: Same as the Silver Star Glacier route to Burgundy Col and onto the glacier (see that route for full trailhead-to-glacier detail), then trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Silver Star Glacier approach
Loose alpine rock typical of Golden Horn batholith summits

waysIn.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your last reliable water until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing: log can be wet or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread easy to lose in the timber; no water between creek and bench
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into Burgundy Col
Loose alpine rock on the summit

waysIn.name: Silver Star Creek from the north
waysIn.notes: Park where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek and follow the trail up the east side of the creek for about two miles. Where it fades near 4,850 ft, trend west across the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire and onto the glacier. Best on continuous spring snow, when it makes a good ski or snowshoe approach; once the valley melts out it turns brushy and swampy and Burgundy Col is the better choice.
hazards: Valley turns brushy and swampy once the snow melts out; best on continuous spring snow
Tread fades near 4,850 ft; cross the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire
Crevasses on the Silver Star Glacier approach
Loose alpine rock on the summit
waysIn.whyThisWay: In spring on continuous snow, as a ski or snowshoe approach that avoids the steep Burgundy Col slope; longer, and once the valley melts out it turns brushy and swampy.

name: West Face Couloir
approach: Approach via the Gato Negro descent gully on Whine Spire; 2-3 hours, snowshoes recommended in early-season snow.
descent: From the west summit, traverse/descend to join the Silver Star Glacier route and follow it back over Burgundy Col to the approach trail.
hazards: Steep, narrow couloir subject to spindrift/rockfall/avalanche
Crux chockstone (M4) has minimal to no protection

name: North Face
approach: Follow the same multi-day approach as the Southwest Route to a high camp on Itswoot Ridge or near the Dome Glacier, then continue over the Dome-Chickamin Glacier col (~8,500 ft) and descend onto the Chickamin Glacier, traversing beneath Sinister's north side to reach the base of the face. The original 1980 first ascent instead approached from the Blizzard-Gunsight col, traversing the Chickamin Glacier from the west. The Downey Creek trail grows muddy, brushy and tangled with deadfall toward Bachelor Creek, then stays rooty and slick for hours until the basin below the ridge.
descent: Most parties downclimb the moderating upper snow slopes and pick an easier walk-off line (often via the west ridge) rather than reverse the full face; the line has also been skied. Return via the Chickamin and Dome Glaciers to Itswoot Ridge and out the Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trails.
hazards: Bergschrund/crevasse hazard at the base of the face
Sustained 45-50 degree snow/ice with few natural anchor options for much of the climb
Icefall from Sinister's upper slopes onto the glacier approach

waysIn.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
waysIn.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
waysIn.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.
hazards: the same ford, avalanche-debris zone and brushy climbers' path as the standard approach
a descent onto a large crevassed icefield with the return climb still to come
a long traverse beneath a face, exposed to anything coming off it
a bergschrund at the base of the face
a shaded north aspect that holds hard ice and cold, with a committing position
an approach that reaches its base by losing height, so retreat means re-climbing

waysIn.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
waysIn.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
waysIn.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.
hazards: long committed glacier travel with no camp of its own
crevasses across the whole traverse
exposure beneath a face for the length of the approach
a bergschrund at the foot of the wall
a plan that only makes sense inside a larger traverse, so a retreat is a multi-day proposition
waysIn.whyThisWay: When already high in the range on a multi-peak traverse, a party can reach the face from the west col across the icefield instead of walking in from the valley for this climb alone.

name: Southwest Route
approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (elev. ~1,450') on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26), follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles (easy, well-graded, mostly flat, forested trail with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek) to Sixmile Camp (2,440'), a good first-night camp with reliable water from Downey Creek. From Sixmile Camp the maintained trail ends; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek initially and fording to the south side around the 9.5-mile mark (~3,700') — treat this as a real creek crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water/early season. Around 4,500' the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone (a major slide wiped out this stretch in 2002); expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber here even in good conditions, and continuous snow well below this elevation in early season. Above the debris zone the path climbs to a pass (~5,900') just northwest of Cub Lake (about 14 miles in), then drops to Cub Lake (5,338', another good camp with water). Most parties push on from Cub Lake up onto Itswoot Ridge (6,400–6,900', ~15 miles and ~5,500' of gain from the trailhead) for high camp, with sweeping views of Dome and Sinister. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins (staying near 7,000') to gain the Dome Glacier, cross over the Dome–Chikamin col, and descend the Chikamin Glacier (crevassed — rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear) to about 7,200'. Traverse right (east) across the glacier to reach the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col; a bergschrund here can be difficult to cross in late season and has occasionally required a short rappel to get down onto or across it (see descent notes — same feature is encountered both ways). From the col, contour on an easy snowfield and climb up into a loose, unpleasant gully on Sinister's south side to gain the upper west ridge, then follow a Class 2–3 scramble along the ridge to the 8,444' summit; some parties instead take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col. Loose rock in the gully is the main climbing-specific hazard on the approach to the summit block.
descent: Reverse the ascent line. Most parties downclimb the same loose south-side gully back to the Dome–Sinister col — it is one of the loosest, most unpleasant sections on the mountain, so expect care-intensive downclimbing with real rockfall risk to anyone below. A commonly preferred alternative, used by several recent parties instead of re-descending the gully, is to descend via the lower west ridge: a newer, more direct line involving sustained Class 3–4 scrambling on semi-solid rock with considerable exposure. One crux move on this ridge variant has a fixed sling left in place for protection/handline use, but this is not a rappel station — parties downclimb through it. Either way, the descent rejoins the gentle snow slopes leading back to the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col. At the col, the bergschrund that guards access to the Chikamin Glacier can be broken/unbridged in mid-to-late season; when it is, parties have used a single rappel (one 60m rope) off natural anchors (rock horn/sling or v-thread in snow, depending on conditions) to get down onto the glacier safely rather than risk a fall into the schrund — in good snow conditions or earlier in the season this same spot is often just a step-across or short downclimb with no rope work needed. From the glacier, re-ascend roughly 1,000' back to the Dome–Chikamin col, then descend to high camp on Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and reverse the long Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully, exposure on the west-ridge variant, and crevasse hazard on the Chikamin/Dome glacier crossings in both directions.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the SW summit gully — one documented ascent involved dodging basketball-size rocks
Crevasses on the Dome/Chickamin Glacier crossing to reach the Dome-Sinister col
Bachelor Creek ford at ~3,700 ft can be hazardous in high water or early-season snowmelt
Long, remote, no-cell-coverage approach with no easy bail-out

waysIn.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
waysIn.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
waysIn.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat

waysIn.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
waysIn.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
waysIn.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col
waysIn.whyThisWay: Parties who want reliable water and a more sheltered camp, or are tired or facing weather after the pass, stop at the lake instead of pushing on to the exposed ridge.

name: Skeena26
