approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached via the same Darrington-area approach: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, follow the rough, unmaintained climbers' approach — the old roadbed past a landslide crossing to a boot track that drops to a ford of Squire Creek, then a climbers' track across a tributary and up through old-growth forest into two steep, dirty gullies that top out on the grassy saddle below the South Face, roughly 3 hours from the car, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Rappel the line of ascent; 50-meter ropes are adequate for most pitches, while 60-meter ropes allow combining pitches 5 and 6 to speed the descent.
hazards: Steep, brushy, poorly maintained approach with a creek ford and old rockslide/avalanche debris
Remote location extends any self-rescue or evacuation timeline

waysIn.name: Squire Creek washout to the west saddle
waysIn.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the Squire Creek ford has dropped; the wall itself faces south-southwest and takes direct sun only through the middle of the day
waysIn.notes: Drive Squire Creek Road out of Darrington until the washout blocks it and park at the gate. Follow the old roadbed past the landslide crossing, watching for two cut logs on either side of the road with old logging cable visible, where a well-established boot track drops right toward the creek. Ford Squire Creek at its shallowest point, follow the climbers' track upstream across a tributary, then climb through two gullies on steep, muddy tread until the ground opens at the grassy saddle below the wall.
hazards: The Squire Creek ford is difficult in early season
Faint, flagged approach track through alder and streambed with several places to lose it
The bolts on the first pitch are old and hard to see against the pale stone

name: South Slopes Scramble
approach: From the Stevens Pass Ski Area's north (uphill) lot, walk to the far east end of the parking area near the small gray electrical substation/WSDOT building — this is the unsigned Skyline Lake trailhead. In summer, take the gravel service road on the left side of the substation, passing beneath the powerlines; a steeper, faster boot path also splits off directly across from the WSDOT building for hikers who want to skip the road switchbacks. Follow the road/track uphill, staying left, then bear right shortly after — a vehicle gate blocks the road about a quarter mile up. The road/trail climbs steadily (roughly 500 ft of gain per half-mile in the steepest stretch) through forest and talus for about 1.2-1.3 miles to Skyline Lake (~1,100-1,300 ft gained, lake sits around 4,900-5,100 ft). Pass Skyline Lake on its south side. Just before the ground steepens into the first rocky scrambling, watch for a large boulder garden — car- to house-sized blocks — and angle southwest through/around it to regain forest on the far side; this talus-hopping section is the main route-finding wrinkle on the whole approach and is slow and ankle-twisty when wet or snow-covered. Beyond the boulder garden, gain the undulating east ridge of the horseshoe-shaped Skyline/Heather Ridge and follow it west, traversing beneath a band of rocky outcrops before the final push to Sky Mountain's summit block. Total one-way distance to the true summit is about 2.5 miles with roughly 1,400-2,600 ft of cumulative gain depending on how much of the undulating ridge is counted (the route re-gains elevation repeatedly along the ridge, which is why the recorded gain (2,600 ft) runs higher than the simple lake-to-summit elevation difference). There is no reliable water past Skyline Lake, so treat/carry water from there. The exposed south-facing slopes below the ridge are a known avalanche path — several fatal slides have occurred here in winter — so this route is best done in summer/early autumn when snow-free; a faint climbers' path is reported to persist most of the way to the summit in those conditions.
descent: This is a walk-off, non-technical scramble descent — no rappelling. Reverse the ascent line: drop off the summit block back onto the undulating east ridge, traverse back beneath the rock outcrops, and pick your way back down through the boulder garden (take care with route-finding here in fog or late in the day, since the talus field has no single obvious line). From the boulder garden, regain the trail/road past Skyline Lake's south shore and descend the service road/boot path back to the Stevens Pass ski area north lot. Stay alert on the ridge and the open south-facing slopes for wind-loaded snow or wet, loose rock; the ridge's minor ups and downs mean the descent regains and loses elevation a few times rather than being a straight shot down.
hazards: Loose, blocky talus and rockfall on the Skyline/Heather Ridge crest, especially at the 'Rock Garden' and the rocky outcrop below the true summit
Faint, unsigned boot path beyond Skyline Lake — easy to lose in fog, at dusk, or under early/late-season snow
Steep heather/talus traverse on the south side of the ridge just below the true summit, with real runout on a slip
Minimal shade on the south-facing approach slopes — heat and sun exposure in mid-summer
Fast-building Cascade-crest afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer

waysIn.name: Skyline Lake and the boulder garden
waysIn.season: July to October
waysIn.notes: The start is unsigned: walk to the far east end of the Stevens Pass north lot, beside the small grey utility building, and take the gravel service road on its left beneath the powerlines. A steeper, faster boot path splits off directly across from that building and skips the road switchbacks. Stay left, then bear right shortly after; a vehicle gate blocks the road about a quarter mile up. Roughly 1.2 miles of steady climbing through forest and talus reaches Skyline Lake, which is the last water — carry what you need from there.
hazards: Loose, blocky talus in the boulder garden and along the ridge crest
Faint boot path beyond the lake, easy to lose in fog or at dusk
Steep heather and talus traverse below the true summit with real runout on a slip
Known avalanche terrain on the exposed south-facing slopes in winter
Little shade and no water past the lake

name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face
peak: Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower
approach: From either trailhead, climbers first gain the Pacific Crest Trail — via the Tunnel Creek Trail climbing about 1,170 ft in 1.45 miles to Hope Lake, or via the Surprise Creek Trail to Surprise Lake — then follow the PCT to Trap Pass (~5,800 ft), south from Hope Lake or north from the Surprise Lake side. From Trap Pass an unmaintained climbers' trail continues south along the ridge to the base of Slippery Slab Tower, with Thunder Mountain further along the same ridgeline above Glacier Lake. The round trip is long enough (roughly 6 miles one-way) that many parties camp overnight at Hope Lake or Trap Lake.
descent: From the summit, make two rappels down the climbing route to return to the base of the tower. Climbers typically use a 60m rope doubled for each rappel, or make multiple 30-50m single-strand rappels. Be mindful of loose, pointy rocks during the descent. Once back at the base, scramble back through the pass terrain to Trap Pass, then reverse the PCT and Tunnel Creek Trail descent.
hazards: Loose, deteriorating black rock on upper sections of pitch 2
Significant exposure on summit slab section during descent
Weather variability and rapid condition changes in the Cascades
Mosquitoes in early summer, especially July, can be severe in lake basins
Snow persistence on approach trail into July despite summer season

waysIn.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
waysIn.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
waysIn.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
hazards: Unmaintained, unsigned ridge path beyond the pass
No water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
Loose, deteriorating black rock on upper pitch 2 and on the ridge approach
Slick granite when wet
Snow persists on the approach trail into July; mosquitoes severe in lake basins in early summer
Two rappels back to the base; loose pointy rocks and exposure on the summit slab
Long round trip commits a day attempt to a late finish

waysIn.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
waysIn.season: July through September
waysIn.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
hazards: More climbing than the crest-trail option, entirely in forest with little view of weather ahead
Unmaintained, unsigned ridge path beyond the pass
No water on the ridge beyond the pass
Loose, deteriorating black rock on upper pitch 2
Slick granite when wet
Snow persists on the approach into July; mosquitoes in lake basins in early summer
Two rappels back to the base; loose pointy rocks and exposure on the summit slab
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a shorter walk to the pass, or to make a relaxed two-day trip with camping at Surprise Lake, accepting more climbing and a shadier, buggier trail.

name: Corkscrew Route
approach: Most parties start from the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,800 ft, at the end of a rough high-clearance spur (Forest Road 4096) off the Mountain Loop Highway a mile or so past the Bedal campground. Follow the Bedal Creek trail through old-growth forest and along the creek to where a large washout has taken the tread; scramble the washout to a cairned exit, then climb the climbers' path through forest and onto talus and meadow to the saddle near 5,300 ft, the last dependable water. From there bear toward the moraine and the lower glacier. A second, less used approach starts from the pullout on Sloan Creek Road and fords the North Fork Sauk River, then follows Cougar Creek; it avoids the Bedal road, but the crossings are dangerous in high water, mainly May through July.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the short, low-5th-class/exposed Class 4 step about 100 ft below the true summit (the 'bear hug' move on the ridge has solid hand cracks on both sides and is usually downclimbed free by competent parties). Parties uncomfortable downclimbing it can rig a short hand line or single-strand rappel here — there is no fixed/bolted anchor; build off a rock horn, chockstone, or gear placement, and a single 30 m/60 m rope doubled is more than enough for the ~15-20 ft of steep rock involved. Below that, follow cairns and the climbers' trail back along the south-face heather ledges and the loose scree/dirt gully that gained access from the ledge system — this gully is notably loose underfoot and the ledges above it have real exposure (parties have noted a ~500 ft unprotected drop at the outer edge), so downclimb it carefully rather than glissading or rushing. At the base of the gully/ledges, re-rope for the glacier crossing back to the toe where gear was staged, then continue down slabs to the basin/saddle. From there it's a full reversal of whichever approach was used — steep scree/slab and forest switchbacks back to the Cougar Creek waterfall and North Fork Sauk crossings (Sloan Creek/FR 49 approach), or the Bedal Creek climbers' path and old trail (Bedal Creek/FS 4096 approach) — down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no standard rappelling on the glacier or ledges; the only rope use besides glacier travel is the optional short hand line/rappel off the summit step described above. Total car-to-car time for strong parties runs roughly 9-13 hours depending on approach and conditions; snow lingering on the basin/ledges into early summer, and afternoon softening of the glacier snowpack on hot days, are the main descent-timing hazards.
hazards: Difficult/dangerous North Fork Sauk River ford (no bridge)
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block
Wet, heavy Cascade snow — high avalanche danger on the approach in spring/early season

Loose rock in the upper Corkscrew gully is a recurring hazard, worse when parties are stacked in the gully; a documented accident (1998) involved a climber falling into a moat on the adjacent Sloan Glacier

waysIn.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
waysIn.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
hazards: Rough, narrow FR 4096 spur; high clearance helps
Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in a brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident

waysIn.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
waysIn.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
waysIn.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk: deep, cold and fast in early season; log jams move year to year
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident
waysIn.whyThisWay: Later in July and August when the river is low, or when the rough spur to the Bedal trailhead is impassable; the traditional approach, but with log crossings and brushy tread.

name: Standard Route (Southwest Slopes)
approach: Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Rd (NW Forest Pass required at the trailhead kiosk). Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead, but instead of taking that trail, look for an unsigned boot path/old roadbed about 50 ft downhill (south) of the Snow Lake trailhead sign, dropping into a band of slide alder — this is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain. The path immediately steepens and follows a creek drainage (Source Creek) up through roots, talus, and brush; it is a climbers' path only, not a maintained trail, and can be hard to follow in the alder in early season or after blowdown. At roughly 1 mile / ~1,000 ft gain, a junction splits: the right fork climbs to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge proper, while the main Snoqualmie route continues left/straight. About a third of a mile past that junction the path fords the creek near a 50-ft waterfall (the main water source on route — treat before drinking); a quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing gully/slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks steeply up this slope for roughly the final mile to the summit ridge and the true summit at 6,278 ft. Expect loose scree and dirt underfoot throughout, exposure on the last stretch of ridge before the top, and lingering snow in the gully well into summer — an ice axe and traction are commonly carried into June. Total is about 3.8 miles round trip with 3,100+ ft of gain, though it is sometimes given as closer to 5 miles depending on exactly where mileage is measured from.
descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel route — descend by reversing the ascent gully/climbers' path back down through Cave Ridge's west slope, past the waterfall creek crossing and the Guye Peak junction, to the Alpental lot. No rappelling or fixed anchors are involved (rappels = 0). The descent is the crux for many parties: the scree/dirt path is looser and harder to control on the way down than it looks going up, and the upper gully holds snow into summer, so in spring conditions a glissade down the snow-filled chute is a common (faster) alternative to the dry boot path — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest if attempting it, since the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down. In winter and spring this same gully is recognized avalanche terrain (a frequent subject of NWAC-relevant trip reports and Mountaineers winter scramble/ski trip logs), so check avalanche conditions and be prepared to bail to Cave Ridge rather than push through unstable snow. Watch footing carefully near the top where the ridge narrows and exposure increases just below the summit.
hazards: Steep, loose, unmaintained climbers' path — easy to kick rock onto parties below, especially in a group
Snow commonly lingers in the upper gully/switchbacks into July — an ice axe (and the skill to use it) may be needed for early-season ascents
Exposed 4th-class step required to reach the true (east) summit; the west/trail summit is about 3 ft lower and far less exposed
Avalanche hazard on the approach slopes in winter and spring — Alpental ski patrol conducts control work nearby

waysIn.name: The unsigned boot path 50 ft below the Snow Lake trailhead sign
waysIn.season: Late July to September for a snow-free scramble; the upper gully commonly holds snow into July. Also climbed as a winter and spring snow route by parties competent to assess avalanche danger
waysIn.notes: Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk. Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead but do not take that trail. About 50 ft downhill (south) of the Snow Lake sign, an unsigned boot path and old roadbed drops into a band of slide alder. That is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain. The path steepens at once and follows the Source Creek drainage through roots, talus and brush. At roughly a mile and 1,000 ft of gain a junction splits — the right fork goes to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge, and the Snoqualmie route continues left and straight. A third of a mile past that the path fords the creek by a 50 ft waterfall, the main water on route. A quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks up it for the final mile. About 3.8 miles round trip with 3,100 ft of gain, though accounts differ on where the mileage is measured from.
hazards: A steep, loose, unmaintained climbers' path — easy to kick rock onto a party below
Snow lingering in the upper gully and switchbacks into July; an axe and the skill to use it may be needed
An exposed fourth-class step to reach the true east summit
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes in winter and spring, with ski patrol control work nearby
The descent is looser and harder to control than the ascent; the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down, which matters if you glissade

name: Neve Glacier / Standard Route
approach: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead (~1,150-1,200 ft, a signed gravel pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, about 21 miles east of Marblemount just past the Diablo turnoff), follow the well-maintained Pyramid Lake Trail as it climbs steadily through old-growth forest. A rock-hop creek crossing at roughly 1 mile is the last easy, reliable water before the lake. At 2.1 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain you reach Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft) - top off water here, since the next several hours offer little. From the lake's south/right side, pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' path; it is steep and brushy from the outset and gains roughly 2,000 ft more, switchbacking up to the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak (~4,000 ft), then follows the narrow, knolly ridge crest past Point 4,555 ft toward Pyramid Peak, with loose rock and short routefinding steps. Just short of Pyramid Peak, descend slightly and traverse - often on lingering snow - across scree and boulders to the terminal moraine and small lake at the base of the Colonial Glacier (~5,900-6,100 ft), the standard first camp, with a tarn for water. From camp, rope up for glacier travel (crevasses present) and climb the Colonial Glacier south to the broad Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,900 ft; a stream/waterfall here is a second good camp and water source), then descend about 200 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it - a moderate, usually well-tracked but crevassed glacier crossing requiring a rope - to the rocks just below Snowfield's summit pyramid on its northwest side. From there a long class 3 gully leads to a notch below the true summit; the final short traverse/scramble across the notch to the south side and up to the summit (8,351 ft) is exposed class 3, with one move occasionally rated low class 4. Given roughly 7,300 ft of total gain and sustained glacier travel, most parties treat this as a 2-day (overnight) objective rather than a single push.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following an independent route. From the summit, downclimb the exposed class 3 (occasionally low class 4) notch and gully back down to the rocks above the Neve Glacier, then retrace the glacier crossing - roped, watching for crevasses and softening snow bridges later in the day - back up to the Colonial-Neve col. From the col, descend the Colonial Glacier (many parties glissade its moderate snow slopes where safe, keeping clear of its crevasses) back to the moraine-lake camp, then reverse the climbers' path and ridge crest over Point 4,555 ft down to Pyramid Lake, finishing on the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail back to the trailhead. In standard summer conditions this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required - the summit notch is a class 3 downclimb reversed on the way out. In early-season, icy, or thin-snow conditions, however, parties have rappelled the notch instead of downclimbing it: one winter party describes building a two-picket snow anchor and making a single-strand rappel with a 30m rope (noting 30m was plenty of length for that pitch), then prusiking back up the same line on their return ascent. Treat that rappel as conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route - there are no bolted or fixed anchors anywhere on this route, so a party that might need it should carry a picket or two and a single 30m-or-longer rope as a contingency. Primary descent hazards are crevasse fall on both the Colonial and Neve glaciers (rope up and probe softening snow bridges, especially in the afternoon), loose rock on the ridge and gully sections, and North Cascades whiteout/navigation risk - the Pyramid Peak ridge and glacier crossings have few visual reference points in cloud, so many parties track their ascent line with GPS for the return.
hazards: Crevasses on the Neve and Colonial Glaciers, worse as the season progresses and snowbridges deteriorate
Steep, dry climbers' trail with no water between Pyramid Lake and the Colonial Glacier basin
Loose rock and occasional verglas/snow on the class 3-4 summit scramble
Routefinding in fog/whiteout on the glacier and ridge
Long, sustained approach (talus, brush, elevation gain) that outweighs the technical climbing in difficulty

waysIn.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
waysIn.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season

waysIn.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
waysIn.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
waysIn.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge
waysIn.whyThisWay: In settled weather with a sound glacier, a party carries overnight loads over the ice to camp at the col for a much shorter summit day, rather than stopping at the moraine.

name: Standard Route / Snowking Glacier
approach: Drive Cascade River Road ~14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn right onto FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road). The road crosses the Cascade River on a concrete bridge; within roughly 0.4 mile the right fork is blocked by boulders/washout and parking is at that Y-junction (around 1,160-1,200ft). From here the true 'approach' begins as a road-walk: follow the closed roadbed (windfall, brush encroachment, washouts that keep it permanently closed to vehicles) for about 2-3 miles, gaining roughly 1,000ft, to a small clearing/end-of-road firepit near 2,300ft. Watch on the left for a steep, easy-to-miss climbers' path leaving the old roadbed into the trees - this is unsigned and has no official trail number. The path climbs steeply through brush and then old-growth forest on a boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no reliable water until well upslope, so top off at the last Cascade River-side crossing if possible. Around 4,800ft there's a boggy bench with a tent spot (first realistic camp/rest option and an intermittent water source). Near 5,200ft the path forks at a signed-by-cairn junction where a fainter 'fisherman's trail' drops toward Found Lake; stay right/uphill on the climbers' path, which steepens over Point 5,791 and follows the Kindy Ridge crest past Found Peak (~5,400ft) and Point 5,695. The ridge undulates - expect several short ups and downs rather than continuous gain - before dropping slightly to the meadows and tarn on the east side of Cyclone Lake (roughly 5,500-6,200ft), the standard high camp with reliable water and the best campsites on the route. From camp, traverse below or over Peak 5,860 heading toward Snowking's east side, then gain the Snowking Glacier proper. In late season this is a straightforward snow/heather slope (~1,900ft over about 1.3 miles to the summit), but by mid-to-late summer the glacier opens up with exposed blue ice and real crevasses - rope up for glacier travel and carry basic crevasse-rescue gear rather than treating it as a snow plod. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip (car to Cyclone Lake camp, then summit day), though strong parties in good conditions do it car-to-car in 12-14 hours.
descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the Snowking Glacier/east-ridge line back toward Cyclone Lake. This is a walk-off, not a rappelling route - no fixed anchors or rappels are typically needed on the standard line, so plan on downclimbing and glacier travel rather than roped lowers. The main hazard is timing: by afternoon, sun-softened, sun-cupped snow bridges over the glacier's crevasses become unreliable, so descend the icy/crevassed upper section earlier in the day if possible and keep the rope team spread out and probing rather than following a single boot track blindly. Below the glacier, pick your way back over/around Peak 5,860 to the Cyclone Lake meadows (camp), then reverse the Kindy Ridge undulations over Point 5,791, Found Peak, and Point 5,695, staying right at the 5,200ft junction to avoid dropping toward Found Lake on the fisherman's trail. From the 4,800ft boggy bench, follow the boot path back down through old growth and brush to the old FR-1570 roadbed, then road-walk the final 2-3 miles out to the car at the washout/gate. Loose duff, roots, and brush on the steep upper boot path are the main footing hazards on the way down; there is no technical rock descent or established rappel sequence on this route.
hazards: Crevasses on the Snowking Glacier, increasingly exposed by late summer
Long, brushy, poorly marked lower approach before the flagged climbers' trail firms up
Washed-out FR-1570 adds significant extra approach mileage and elevation gain
Afternoon cloud/whiteout over the broad, featureless glacier plateau can make navigation difficult

waysIn.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
waysIn.season: June through September
waysIn.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return

waysIn.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
waysIn.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
waysIn.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
waysIn.whyThisWay: When a shorter summit day matters more than shelter, a party goes on to the wind-exposed benches above the lake instead of camping at the meadows.

name: South Arete
approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (elev. ~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-built Blue Lake Trail (Trail #314) as it climbs gently through subalpine fir and larch forest, switchbacking up open slabs with good views back at the highway. After roughly 1.3-1.5 miles and about 1,000 ft of gain, watch for a minor stream crossing/drainage coming down from the basin below the Early Winter Spires — this is well before Blue Lake itself, which lies another mile-plus further on the maintained trail. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the climbers' boot path (cairned but braided in spots) that works up through granite slabs and heather benches, then continues up open talus and boulder country roughly parallel to the stream, which is a reliable water source through most of the season lower down but disappears into talus higher up — fill up before leaving it. Continue up this climbers' trail, angling toward the southwestern corner/toe of South Early Winter Spire (the right-hand, southernmost of the two spires, before the saddle). Expect roughly another 1,000 ft of gain from where you leave the maintained trail to reach the base of the route at the level of the North/South spire saddle, for a total of about 2.5 hours and up to ~2,000 ft of gain from the car. The path is mostly straightforward but loses definition on the upper talus and slab benches — trend toward the obvious southwest corner of the spire rather than chasing any single cairn line, and take care on the granite slabs low down when wet or covered in old snow, which can persist into early summer in shaded gullies. At the fork higher on the trail, the right branch heads for the Early Winter Spires and the left one for Liberty Bell.
descent: Descend by rappelling/downclimbing the South Arete climbing route itself. In recent years the route has been equipped with three fixed rappel stations (bolts and chains) set slightly climber's right of the summer gully/chimney and off the main line of ascent, giving clean, mostly-vertical pulls; a single 60m rope is sufficient for each rappel and gets you back to the base of the route in 2-3 rappels, supplemented by short sections of easy downclimbing between stations depending on how much you choose to downclimb versus rappel. Because some of the down-climbing is exposed with real fall consequences, parties newer to alpine terrain should stay roped and consider placing gear on the downclimbed sections rather than soloing them. From the base of the raps, reverse the approach: pick up the climbers' trail back down through the talus and slabs paralleling the stream to the Blue Lake Trail, then follow it back to the trailhead. An alternative descent used by some parties is to traverse to the Southwest Couloir and downclimb/walk that gully back into the basin instead of re-rapping the arete; it avoids rope work but is loose underfoot and can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and possibly crampons) is warranted.
hazards: Airy, exposed knife-edge ridge sections carry real fall consequence despite the low technical grade
Broad, broken ridge makes it easy to wander off-route

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes

waysIn.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
waysIn.season: Highway opening through Jun
waysIn.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter
waysIn.whyThisWay: From the highway opening through June, when snow still buries the climbers' path in the basin and a party navigates by terrain, using firm morning snow to climb faster.

name: Direct East Buttress
approach: Park at the 'hairpin' pullout on Highway 20 (separate from the Blue Lake Trailhead), hike up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last large tree in the gully, then traverse right across talus (or snow early-season — bring crampons/axe) to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress. Roughly 1.5 hours car-to-base at a moderate pace; the line is visible from the road.
descent: Downclimb the South Arete from the summit — mostly 3rd/4th class with one short, more exposed 5th-class section — down to bolted anchors above the standard SEWS descent gully, then make 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains to the base of the wall. From the base, hike out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail; if you parked at the hairpin rather than the Blue Lake Trailhead, plan a short road walk or car shuttle back.
hazards: sustained hard crack and face pitches
high exposure
afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the right, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach

waysIn.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
waysIn.season: Highway opening through Jun
waysIn.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter
waysIn.whyThisWay: From the highway opening through June, when Spire Gully still holds snow and the traverse is done on snow, with an axe and crampons for the extra firmness.

name: Southwest Couloir
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (1 mile west of Washington Pass on SR-20), head into the woods, break treeline around 5,900 ft, and navigate toward the distinctive Y-shaped snow gully below the South Arete.
descent: Descend the couloir you climbed. From the summit block downclimb the short third-class step, then rappel from the tree anchor just below the summit into the head of the couloir; the steeper, narrower sections lower down are also handled by rappel or downclimbing, depending on how much snow is left. Late in the season the couloir fills with loose class 3-4 rock, which is hard to downclimb and sends rockfall onto anyone below, so it is best done while snow still covers it. Once out of the couloir, walk down the open slope and the snow-covered approach to the Blue Lake trailhead.
hazards: Rockfall in late-season, snow-free conditions
Avalanche hazard on the approach in spring

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail into the west basin (snow)
waysIn.season: A few weeks to a couple of months after SR-20 reopens — roughly May-Jun
waysIn.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the main trail roughly a mile and a half to the well-worn climbers' trail and take it up into the basin on the west side of the Liberty Bell group. Early in the season the trailhead lot itself may still be snowed in.

On a cold morning parties approach in boots and crampons without flotation; later in the day the same snow softens badly. Start early and plan to be off the couloir before the afternoon.

This is the quickest line to the summit of the south spire, and it exists only for a short window: it comes into condition once the highway opens and deteriorates as the snow goes. Late in the season the couloir empties out into loose rock and is not worth climbing.
hazards: avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a sun-affected slope, worsening through the day
snow and occasional ice to around 50 degrees in the upper narrows
late season the couloir fills with loose rock and becomes a rockfall trap — not recommended once melted out
route depends entirely on SR-20 reopening, typically mid-April to early May

name: South Face
approach: From the pullout, find a faint boot path descending loose talus/scree to the east into the trees, passing a trail register, then crossing Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft). The trail climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply gaining elevation to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (roughly 2 hours from the car), then continues up to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft, ~3 hours). Vasiliki Tower rises directly from the north side of the col; good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft.
descent: From the summit, climbers typically descend via the North Ridge, a fun and easy Class 3 scramble back to Burgundy Col. The North Ridge descent takes approximately 1 hour round trip from summit to col. Alternatively, rappel stations may be used for a faster descent.
hazards: Exposure on vertical granite
Rock fall potential from upper sections
Weather hazards at elevation

waysIn.name: Burgundy Creek rib to Burgundy Col
waysIn.season: Midsummer to early autumn. This face takes sun through the day, so it comes into condition earlier and holds later than the shaded sides of the group
waysIn.notes: From the unsigned roadside pullout, find the faint boot path dropping east through loose talus into the trees past a trail register, then cross Early Winters Creek on a log. The path climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply, to a basin bench around 6,400 to 6,500 ft where there is good camping and a late-season spring, then continues up scree and snow to Burgundy Col.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to the col
Early Winters Creek log crossing can be awkward at high flow
Nothing on the approach is signed or marked

name: South Face
approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 24 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: from Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and climb scree/talus to the base of the peak's main South Face and start low in the centre of the open wall, left of the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk (the SE Buttress starts inside that gully).
descent: Descend west off the summit via the regular class-3 walk-up route, the same descent used by the NE Ridge route; involves loose talus and some downclimbing back toward camp.
hazards: Remote big-wall-style granite route, far from rescue — self-rescue capability required
Afternoon thunderstorms common in the North Cascades interior in summer

waysIn.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
waysIn.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
waysIn.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
hazards: Roughly 12-mile trail approach to Andrews Pass, over an old burn that is hot, rocky and buggy with no shade
Several routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat

waysIn.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
waysIn.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
waysIn.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
Wall foreshortens from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
Loose rock and grainy granite in places
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat
waysIn.whyThisWay: For the shortest walk and least total climbing, for parties who accept a drive about two hours longer and roughly 1,300 ft of uphill on the way out.

waysIn.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
waysIn.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Very long approach: Chewuch River trail nearly to Remmel Lake, then a climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin
Loose rock and grainy granite in places; rockfall from parties above
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat
waysIn.whyThisWay: When combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb, as a longer way round than the Andrews Creek trail.

name: South Face
approach: From the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead (Bean Creek/Beverly Creek TH) off the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR-9737-112), the approach is well-documented with concrete checkpoints: at about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike Trail) — a wrong fork onto the Bean Creek Trail here is a commonly reported mistake, so double-check the sign. At about 2.8 miles, at a faint fork in a grove of trees, turn right onto Trail #1218 (Fourth Creek Trail). About 0.3 mile later you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. Continue down the far side to about 6 miles and ~4,200 ft, where you ford Ingalls Creek (wading or a footlog) to reach good flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence — day one is roughly 6 miles and 2,000 ft of gain. From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west for about half a mile, then cut sharply left (north) and start climbing straight upslope toward Argonaut's south face: expect brushy 'jackstraw' forest for the first 300 vertical feet and then dense slide alder for close to 1,000 feet above that (progress can slow to a few hundred feet per hour in the thick of it — stay right/climber's-right to minimize brush where possible). At about 5,200 ft the brush relents onto open slopes; ascend the left side of a large drainage gully up to about 6,600 ft, then continue up the gully itself. At about 7,100 ft the gully forks — the standard line is the left branch (the right also goes but is less traveled). At the base of the summit face, start in the rightmost and larger of two short left-facing corners and climb about three pitches of blocky rock to the summit. The 50-foot chockstone gully that tops out on the east ridge (Class 4, stepping right at the overhang) is the finish of the scramble route, not part of this climb; it is the usual way down. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford, sustained brush-bashing on the lower slopes, and possible snow in the gully in shoulder season (carry an axe/crampons if conditions warrant).
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent gully. The single technical obstacle is the 50-foot chockstone gully near the top: rappel it rather than downclimbing (a webbing/sling anchor is typically found immediately above the chockstone — inspect and consider backing it up with fresh webbing, as reports note it sees heavy wear). A 40 m rope is ideal for this rappel and a 30 m rope will also reach; be careful feeding/pulling the rope past the chockstone, as trip reports specifically warn the rope can get stuck on it and that a pendulum is possible if you're off to one side. Below the chockstone, downclimb the gully and continue down through the two gully forks and open slopes back to about 5,200 ft, then re-enter the brush band and pick your way back down through the slide alder and jackstraw forest to the Ingalls Creek Trail. Reverse the approach from there: re-ford Ingalls Creek, climb back over Fourth Creek Pass, and follow Trail #1226.1/#1391 back to the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead. This is a full, long descent day (figure roughly 4 hours from summit back to camp) — start down with a solid daylight margin.
hazards: Extended off-trail travel through brush and talus on approach

waysIn.name: Beverly Turnpike and Fourth Creek Pass to an Ingalls Creek camp, then straight up the south side
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The brush is the reason: it is impassably wet in early season and the gully may hold snow in the shoulders
waysIn.notes:
From the Beverly Turnpike trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 off the North Fork Teanaway Road, at about 0.5 mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391. Taking the Bean Creek fork here is a commonly reported mistake, so read the sign.

At about 2.8 miles, at a faint fork in a grove of trees, turn right onto Trail #1218, the Fourth Creek Trail; about 0.3 mile later you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to roughly 6 miles and 4,200 ft, ford Ingalls Creek, and camp at the Fourth Creek confluence. Day one is about 6 miles and 2,000 ft.

From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile, then cut sharply left and north and climb straight upslope. Expect roughly 300 vertical feet of tangled forest and then close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above that — progress can drop to a few hundred feet an hour.

At about 5,200 ft the brush relents. Climb the left side of a large drainage gully to about 6,600 ft, then the gully itself.
hazards: Close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above 300 ft of jackstraw forest — the defining feature of the day
An Ingalls Creek ford that can be cold and swift early, and ice-covered in the shoulders
Loose blocks low on the route
Possible snow in the gully in the shoulder seasons — carry axe and crampons if in doubt
The descent rappels a chockstone gully where ropes are reported to hang up on the chockstone
A heavily worn sling anchor above that chockstone: inspect and back it up

name: South Face
approach: From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166 (0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff), the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately (around 4,080 ft, via logs), and climbs steeply — gaining nearly 2,400 ft — to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to 7,770-ft Burgundy Col. Rather than dropping straight to Pernod's south side from the col, most parties continue traversing/scrambling around the east (Silver Star Creek) side of the ridge below Chianti, aiming for the notch between Pernod and Chablis — expect loose 4th-class terrain on this stretch. Because the South Face is short (Grade II, 2 pitches, 5.9) and sits tucked between Pernod's bigger west face and Chablis, many parties approach it as a linkup: climb Chablis' East Face first, then downclimb or make a short rappel across loose rock to reach the base of Pernod's south face rather than committing to the full traverse from Burgundy Col. Either way, carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
descent: This is not a walk-off — the way down is by rappel. From the summit area, one commonly used anchor is a two-piton station equalized with cord; the short aid block just below the top is protected by a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger — treat the old bolt with real suspicion. Rappel the south face to the Pernod-Chablis notch on two ropes (60m ropes recommended; a single 70m can just barely work, but a 60m single can leave you several meters short of the notch). Watch for rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station — build that anchor as high as practical so the rope doesn't jam on the pull. From the notch, a short 4th-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis, and two double-rope rappels down that line reach the base, rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col. If you're descending independently instead of via Chablis, reverse the traverse below Chianti back to Burgundy Col and follow the climbers' path down the scree gullies to the bench camp and boot path to the highway.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall potential in the approach gullies and around the notch — typical of the Wine Spires' sometimes-fractured granite
Lingering snow across the approach and notch into July
Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer
Fixed rappel anchors on Washington Pass towers can be old — inspect before weighting (a 2025 anchor failure on nearby North Early Winters Spire was fatal)

waysIn.name: Burgundy Col, then the loose fourth-class traverse round the east side below Chianti to the Pernod-Chablis notch
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately at around 4,080 ft via logs, and climbs steeply, gaining nearly 2,400 ft, to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to Burgundy Col at 7,770 ft.

Two pitches at 5.9 A0, Grade II. Carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
hazards: Loose fourth-class traverse around the east side of the ridge below Chianti
A two-piton summit anchor equalized with cord, and a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger on the short summit aid block
A single 60 m rope can leave a party several metres short of the notch on the descent
Rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station; build that anchor as high as practical
Loose rock underfoot for the whole approach

name: South Face
approach: Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground (~600 ft) and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the highway 20 corridor. The first ~3.75-4 miles follow an old, gently-graded forest roadbed along Goodell Creek — brushy and with some downed logs in the first mile, and crossing two boulder-strewn washout sections where the tread disappears into the creek's flood debris and you pick a line across large boulders (the trickiest routefinding of the lower approach). About 200 yards past the second washout, at an obvious campsite with a fire ring, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed — historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. This is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach. From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest (hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches) and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline, make a rising traverse across meadow, slab, and (early-season) snow to a ~6,200 ft saddle/notch near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft — matching the route's recorded ~7.4 mi / ~5,200-5,800 ft gain figures, and typically a full 6-8 hour day with a pack. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the water source early in the season; by late summer it can be dry and parties melt snow instead. From camp, rope up and cross the Terror Glacier — the icefall in its middle is broken and often has open crevasses; parties commonly work a left-trending snow ramp/ice bridge above a large crevasse to get through it onto gentler slopes beyond, and this crossing gets more serious (more open crevasse, thinner bridges) as the season progresses. Aim for the lower-left corner of the South Face where a small rock buttress meets the glacier — that buttress is the start of the route.
descent: Standard descent rappels the upper West Ridge to a notch, then continues down the South Face to the glacier rather than reversing the Great Gash. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a few hundred feet toward a notch on the ridge, then begin rappelling. Multiple trip reports of this exact route confirm it as a sustained multi-rappel descent through a gully/notch system with no bolts; the stations are fixed pins, nuts and cord of variable quality, slung horns, or anchors built from gear (nuts, small-to-medium cams), so carry a rack sufficient for both the climb and for leaving/building rappel anchors, plus some cord or rap tat. One detailed trip report of this route logged 7 double-rope rappels, about three and a half down the West Ridge and four down the South Face, back to the Terror Glacier, building a fresh natural anchor at each station; a separate party descending the same general line but counting differently (single 70m rope, more, shorter pitches) reported roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge to a notch followed by about 9 more rappels down through the gully/South Face terrain to the glacier, with several rappels traversing hard to one side to reach the next station and the final rappel using nearly the full rope length to reach a flat spot on the ice. Two ropes give the fewest rappels. The two-rope stations sit roughly 60 m apart and a single 70 m rope doubled reaches only about 35 m, so on one rope expect roughly twice as many stations: about 14 rappels of 30-35 m, which is what the single-rope party above ended up doing. Expect loose rock in the gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on the traversing raps, so back up rappels and check pulls carefully. The descent ends back on the Terror Glacier at the base of the West Ridge/South Face, from which you re-cross the icefall (same crevasse hazard as the approach, now on tired legs and possibly softer afternoon snow) to regain camp, then reverse the Terror Basin boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.
hazards: crevassed Terror Glacier on approach
moat where the glacier meets the base of the face
rockfall, particularly from parties above on the shared descent
Terror Glacier crevasse hazard increases later in the season as the glacier 'opens up' (general Picket Range pattern)

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek to the Glee Peak saddle camp, then through the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the lower-left corner of the face
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; the first ascent was made in mid-June in a low-snow year
waysIn.notes: Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground at about 600 ft and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the Highway 20 corridor. That is the trickiest route-finding of the lower approach. About 200 yards past the second washout, at an obvious campsite with a fire ring, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed, historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. That is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach. From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest, hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches, and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline a rising traverse across meadow, slab and early-season snow reaches a saddle or notch at about 6,200 ft near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the early-season water source; by late summer parties melt snow.
hazards: Two boulder-strewn washouts where the tread vanishes, the lower approach's route-finding crux
A broken Terror Glacier icefall with open crevasses that worsens through the season
A camp water source that dries out by late summer
A sustained multi-rappel descent down the West Ridge and then the South Face, with no bolts anywhere on the peak and fixed pin stations of variable quality
Loose rock in the descent gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on traversing rappels

name: South Face
approach: Start at the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North (PCT-Northbound) trailhead off I-90 Exit 52, elevation about 3,000-3,040 ft. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north for roughly 2.5 miles through second-growth forest, climbing gently, to the signed junction with the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033). Follow #1033 into Commonwealth Basin; not far past the junction the trail crosses Commonwealth Creek, which is the last reliable water on the approach and can be a tricky ford in early season/high snowmelt. Immediately beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread - there is no trail from here - and climb cross-country to the northwest, first through open timber and then boulder/talus, gaining roughly 1,500-2,000 ft into the open cirque at the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek beneath Lundin's south face. The face rises directly above; the route starts near the low point of the face, close under the summit. Total car-to-base distance is roughly 3-3.5 miles one-way, with lingering snow patches possible into early summer in the upper basin and some route-finding through talus to find the actual toe of the face.
descent: Descend by scrambling the connecting ridge to the Southeast Ridge and following it down (Class 3-4), the standard descent for routes topping out on Lundin's summit. The ridge crosses several rock horns; between the first two there is a short (~40 ft) Class 3+ downclimb, and lower on the ridge is a single rappel of roughly 25 meters down a step that's awkward to downclimb, from a long-standing fixed anchor (slung chockstones - natural gear, not bolted) that lands you on Class 2 ledges. From there continue down the ridge/talus back toward Red Pass or directly into Commonwealth Basin to rejoin the approach line and the PCT. A single 30m or 60m rope is sufficient for the one rappel; in good, dry conditions some parties downclimb this step instead of rigging a rappel.

waysIn.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; early season on snow is preferred
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead off I-90 exit 52, about 3,000-3,040 ft. Follow the PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles through second-growth, climbing gently, to the signed junction with the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033).

Follow #1033 into Commonwealth Basin. Not far past the junction it crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last reliable water on the approach, and a tricky ford in early season at high snowmelt.

Immediately beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread. There is no trail from here. Climb cross-country to the northwest, first through open timber and then boulder and talus, into the open cirque at the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek beneath Lundin's south face.

An equivalent description used by many parties: stay on the Commonwealth Creek trail until soon after the stream crossing, where it starts moving up onto the flank of Red Mountain, then leave it and head northwest into the basin. Many climbers deliberately come early in the season, when snow covers the brush and boulders and the cross-country leg is quick.
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail from the creek crossing onward - open timber then boulder and talus
lingering snow patches in the upper basin into early summer
route-finding across talus to locate the true toe of the face

name: South Face
approach: Two main approach options: via the Snow Creek trail (leaving it around 3,200 ft) or via the Hook Creek drainage from Icicle Creek Lane. Both lead up to Edward Mesa (the 'Lost World Plateau'), from which climbers descend to the south side of Edward Peak to a steep gully holding a giant chockstone.
descent: Descend either by rappelling off natural anchors (a boulder with slings/bolt, or a horn rappel station) or by downclimbing the ascent line.
hazards: Early-season snow in the approach/summit gully
Ticks on the brushy approach
Loose blocks reported in places typical of rarely-traveled alpine rock

name: South Gully/South Spur
approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
descent: From the south summit, traverse the connecting ridge to Guye's middle summit, then make a roughly 30-meter rappel from slung trees down to the north summit. From there, descend west via the Cave Ridge climbers' trail back toward Alpental, or alternatively east via the Commonwealth Basin trail — this is the shared standard descent for Guye Peak's south-side lines.
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite — climber-triggered rockfall is very likely, and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds.
Rockfall risk multiplies with parties stacked in the gully; a helmet is strongly recommended from the talus field upward.
The gully fills with snow and becomes avalanche-prone in winter and spring — check the NWAC forecast before any early-season attempt.
The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area conducts avalanche blasting on nearby slopes in season; call the resort (425-434-7669) to check before a winter attempt.
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions.

waysIn.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
waysIn.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
waysIn.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds; helmet from the talus upward
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
Huge cliffs on the approach; the start of the gully lies about 100 ft left of them
Whiteout route-finding on the winter approach

waysIn.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
waysIn.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
waysIn.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall very likely with a documented fatal history
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully; helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant
Private property on the walking approach is closed to climbers; no-parking signs on the road
Chockstone and moat problems; verglas on rock in cold shoulder seasons
waysIn.whyThisWay: Once the snow has gone, roughly June to October, when the gully can be scrambled dry from the Alpental road, a looser and lower-consequence outing than the winter climb.

name: South Headwall
approach: Northeast via Ingalls Way Trail #1390 and Longs Pass Trail #1229, then down to Ingalls Creek; ascend first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
descent: The route tops out very close to the true summit, so the way down is the Cascadian Couloir to the south. Cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), then drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek. The headwall base lies up-basin along the same drainage, so collect anything left there, then climb back to Longs Pass and walk out to the Esmeralda trailhead. Carry an ice axe through at least midsummer, and stay out from under other parties, as the couloir is notoriously loose.
hazards: The approach gains the headwall via loose, sandy 3rd-class scree

waysIn.name: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better
waysIn.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
hazards: Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties
Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail
A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions
An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt
