Early-season snow and ice in the cirque
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing

name: South Ridge
approach: Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area/Lake Ann trailhead on SR 20 (milepost ~157.5, elev. ~4,850 ft; 40-car lot with privy). Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (#740) about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass (the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann). Climb through meadows to Heather Pass (~2.6 mi, ~6,100 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus/boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake (~3.5-4 mi, ~5,700 ft; timbered campsites on the north side, water available) — this off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake (~5 mi, ~6,900 ft), the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake and reliable water into late summer. From Wing Lake, go around the right (north) side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus/snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit; climb this gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping out at the south col on the crest of the south ridge — the true start of the climbing.
descent: This is the standard descent line for the peak — no separate down-route to learn. The ascent from the south col follows the cairned ridge (some class 3 moves) and a loose gully just west of the crest to the summit pyramid; the final section is a cairned class 2 ledge system traversing below the summit block that is exposed near its end, followed by a short (~15 ft) class 4 step to the true summit. On the way down, reverse this: downclimb the class 4 step (a boulder slung here permits a short optional rappel or hand-line — a single 30m rope is more than enough rope, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in), reverse the ledge traverse and the gully, and retrace the ridge back to the south col. From the col, descend the scree-and-snow slope (glissade-able early season) back down to Wing Lake, then hike out the approach trail. There is no mandatory multi-pitch rappel sequence on this route; the class 4 summit step is the only spot where climbers occasionally use a rope on the way down.
hazards: loose "ball-bearing" scree just below the south col
rockfall on the two talus fields near Lewis Lake
exposed, cairned class-2 ledge traverse around the summit block
early-season cornices/snow lingering above Heather Pass into July

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the unmarked path past Lewis Lake to Wing Lake
waysIn.season: May-Oct, best Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area and Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 157.5 at about 4,850 ft, a 40-car lot with a privy. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the Lake Ann below Mount Shuksan on the Mount Baker Highway; the two are about 80 km apart and share a name.

Follow the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass; the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann. Climb through meadows to Heather Pass at about 2.6 miles and 6,100 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus and boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake at about 3.5-4 miles and 5,700 ft, with timbered campsites on the north side and water. This off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake at about 5 miles and 6,900 ft, the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake.
hazards: An unmarked off-trail stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake, the approach's main route-finding challenge, worse with cairns buried by snow
Cliff bands directly below the south col if you climb the gully straight up rather than angling right
An exposed cairned ledge traverse below the summit block
A short class 4 step at the summit
Two lakes in Washington named Lake Ann; this route uses the Rainy Pass one

name: South Ridge
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) to the high camp near 7,600 ft on the Inspiration Glacier flat. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. For this specific route: from high camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline seen from camp, below an obvious crack leading up to a U-shaped notch in the crest.
descent: Descend via Eldorado's standard East Ridge route back toward the glacier camp.
hazards: Loose scree/snow conditions after the snow melts out

waysIn.name: Glacier flank traverse from the east ridge camp
waysIn.season: July to September, once the glacier flank snow has consolidated but before the ground above the notch melts out to loose scree
waysIn.notes: From the parking area on Cascade River Road, backtrack along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River, then take the steep unmaintained climbers' boot path up through old-growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine basin above. Camp on the rocks by the broad flat of the glacier — the standard camp for the ordinary east-ridge line — and traverse from there. Overnight stays need a free backcountry permit.
hazards: The traverse to the base is steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier — crampons are mandatory
Ground above the ridge is broad and turns to loose scree when melted out
Glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear is required to reach camp at all

name: South Spur
approach: The standard approach begins at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Hannegan Pass Rd/FS-32 off SR 542, ~3,100 ft), following Hannegan Pass Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (~5,050-5,100 ft). From the pass, the trail switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp, then continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing — a ford that can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow and is the approach's main hazard; check levels before committing, and expect it to be harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle (~5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5-8.5 hours/8-9 miles from the trailhead depending on pace and the ford). From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest of Easy Ridge, over or around Easy Peak (6,613 ft, ascend its south ridge), to the notorious 'Imperfect Impasse' — a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often-wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft down to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs a exposed Class 4 rock step (many parties belay this) to regain the ridge on the far side. Beyond the Impasse the trail continues to Perfect Pass (~6,200 ft), the standard high camp for Whatcom Peak, about 16 miles in from the trailhead, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass itself in late season — plan to fill up at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt. An alternative approach skips Easy Ridge entirely: from Whatcom Pass (reached via the Chilliwack River/Brush Creek trail or the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake — see the North Ridge route for that approach), a 'low orbit' traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields without crossing the Impasse, but it exposes climbers to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier and should be treated as glacier travel (rope/crevasse-rescue gear) in early season. In August the Chilliwack River ford is easy using a log for most of the width, and water is plentiful on Easy Peak up to about 6,000 ft.
descent: This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling involved. From the summit (7,574 ft), reverse the south ridge crest — an exposed Class 3-4 scramble — down to the top of the south-facing snowfield, then descend the snowfield (glissade-able in the right conditions, early-mid season) back to Perfect Pass. From Perfect Pass, most parties simply reverse the Easy Ridge approach (down through the Impasse workaround to Easy Saddle, then out via Hannegan Pass). Parties doing a Picket-range traverse or looping back toward Whatcom Pass instead descend via the low-orbit traverse around the peak's east side, or cross the Whatcom Glacier directly when it is 'in' and consolidated (rope up for glacier travel and watch for moats near the pass) — parties describe this glacier crossing as straightforward in good late-summer conditions but it should not be treated as guaranteed snow-covered/moat-free. No fixed anchors or rappel stations exist on this route; rappels = 0.
hazards: Imperfect Impasse: deep snow moats and wet, down-sloping 4th-class slabs — the real crux of the Easy Ridge approach
Exposed, narrow summit ridge (PG13 rating)
Whatcom Glacier crevasses/moats if using the east-side low-orbit approach
Long, remote, routefinding-intensive approach
Late-August conditions can produce bare ice, open crevasses, and a summit-blocking moat ~5 ft wide that has turned back at least one documented NPS ranger party

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season

waysIn.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
waysIn.notes:
An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
waysIn.whyThisWay: To avoid the Chilliwack ford and the Imperfect Impasse, a party goes round via Whatcom Pass and crosses the river by cable car, accepting a longer walk and a brushy climbers' path.

name: North Ridge
approach: Access is via the Dailey Prairie logging-road network reached from the Middle Fork Nooksack River bridge (~1,200 ft) on the north side of the Twin Sisters Range — the DNR/private gate situation there changes year to year, so treat the drive-in as unverified until confirmed for your trip. From wherever the gate stops you, most parties bike the remaining logging roads (roughly 6-7 miles of climbing/quarry road) to save the return slog, stashing bikes near the old pipe barrier/end-of-road at the base of the western cirque between North Twin and South Twin. From there a climbers' path — brushy, overgrown, and wet but not hard to follow — drops into timber and works southeast, fading into a red talus slope; traverse right (south) across the talus, cross a timbered rib, and pass the ruins of an old log cabin as a landmark. Orsino Creek, crossed along this stretch, is the last reliable water source for the entire climb and camp — fill up here. Beyond the creek the path becomes a steep, unpleasant grind of dirt, scree, and talus into the open basin below the North Twin/South Twin cirque; this slope often holds snow into midsummer, so an ice axe (and, early season, crampons) should be expected. Unlike the standard West Ridge route, which gains the ridge at an obvious notch around 5,200 ft, the North Ridge continues higher and further climber's-left (north) up basin snow or talus to reach the saddle/notch between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge, around 5,800 ft — this saddle is the actual start of the route. Expect route-finding to be the crux of the approach itself: multiple plausible lines exist up the basin headwall depending on snow coverage, and parties have found the basin slog and the final gain to the notch the most tedious part of the day.
descent: Do not reverse the North Ridge to descend — the standard guidance to bail out via the West Ridge instead is well founded: the last ~400 vertical feet of the North Ridge below the summit is steep, exposed low-5th-class terrain on the crest, and reversing it is slower and riskier than descending the standard line. From the summit, join/descend the West Ridge: follow the ridge crest down but do not stay glued to the crest proper through the steep section below the false summit — following the crest exactly can force an improvised rappel. Instead, contour off the crest onto the south side for roughly 200 yards from the false summit, losing about 500 ft, then cut back to rejoin the ridge crest lower down and follow the cairned scramble route down and left (south) to the base of the ridge near the 5,200 ft notch. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent for a party following the correct line — no rappels are required on the standard descent (rappels: 0), though carry a short rap setup as an emergency option if snow/ice conditions or a wrong turn onto the crest force a downclimb none of the party is comfortable reversing. Watch for loose rock and dirt in the bypass gully, and for a snow-filled moat at the base of the gully in early season. Once back down at the basin, retrace the approach: descend to Orsino Creek to refill water, pick up the climbers' path back through the talus and timber, and return to the bikes/logging road for the ride/hike out.
hazards: Loose, crumbly rock on the lower ridge away from the crest
Crevasses and the moat on the Sisters Glacier crossing below the ridge
A late-season moat separating the South Twin summit from the glacier, which can require technical downclimbing or a short rappel to negotiate
Real exposure on low-5th-class sections of the ridge crest
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed, glaciated ridge

waysIn.name: Dailey Prairie roads and Orsino Creek Basin, then higher and left to the 5,800 ft saddle
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Earlier gives firmer snow bridges on the Sisters Glacier and more crevasse-fall risk; later opens the crevasses and widens the moat
waysIn.notes:
Access is via the Dailey Prairie logging-road network from the Middle Fork Nooksack River bridge near 1,200 ft on the north side of the range. The DNR and private gate situation changes year to year, so treat the drive-in as unverified until confirmed.

From wherever the gate stops you, most parties bike roughly 6-7 miles of climbing and quarry road, stashing bikes near the old pipe barrier at the end of road, at the base of the western cirque between North Twin and South Twin.

From there a climbers' path — brushy, overgrown and wet but not hard to follow — drops into timber and works southeast, fading into a red talus slope. Traverse right, south, across the talus, cross a timbered rib, and pass the ruins of an old log cabin. Orsino Creek along this stretch is the last reliable water for the climb and the camp.

Beyond the creek the path becomes a steep grind of dirt, scree and talus into the open basin below the North Twin / South Twin cirque, often holding snow into midsummer.
hazards: Glacier travel on the Sisters Glacier with a moat at the rock margin that widens all season
A basin headwall with multiple plausible lines and none of them obvious
The last 400 ft on the crest, steeper and more exposed than anything below and possibly low fifth class
A documented cliffing-out trap for parties drifting right below the summit
The North Ridge is not reversed on descent — the standard way down is the West Ridge, a different line

name: Southeast Face
approach: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small, unsigned Boston Basin pulloff/trailhead at about 3,200-3,300 ft (a rough, sometimes rutted gravel road best driven with a bit of clearance). From the trailhead, follow the old abandoned mining road for about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, where the road ends and an unmaintained but well-traveled climbers' boot path takes over. This path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams/seasonal creeks (reliable water in early/mid season, so top off bottles here), and reaches treeline around 5,300 ft after roughly 2.5-3 miles and about 3,000 ft of gain. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on a knoll above green meadows at roughly 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day. From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up for glacier travel and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully/couloir below the tower - if a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate entry, rejoining the couloir about 100 ft up. Getting into the correct gully matters: on July 10, 2005, a six-person Mountaineers party mistakenly climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here; during the roped traverse back toward the standard line a climber was struck by rockfall, and minutes later, during the retreat rappel, a natural boulder anchor gave way, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth, so confirm the line (ideally with GPS track or beta photos) before committing, especially in poor visibility. For the Southeast Face specifically, there is no separate approach line to the face itself - parties climb the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge (the block/dihedral pitch to the notch, described in that route) and rappel from a fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2 to reach the base of the Southeast Face's crack pitch. In July the bottom of the approach gully is guarded by a moat, and a short wall of snow must be climbed to reach the chute.
descent: Descent is a combination of short technical rappels off the face followed by the shared Sharkfin descent gully used by all routes on the tower. From the top of the Southeast Face's second pitch, make two 75-foot (~23m) rappels back down to the notch atop Southeast Ridge pitch 1/2 - a single 60m rope doubled is more than adequate for both. The anchors here are bolted but sparse: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains or rap rings, so plan to leave a locking biner, rap ring, or short cord unless you can retrieve gear on the way down; there is no anchor at the very base of pitch 1, so keep the team roped/attentive on that stretch. Once back at the ridge notch, continue down via the same downclimb-and-rappel gully system used to descend the Southeast Ridge (see that route's descent for detail) - expect several more short rappels on natural anchors (chockstones, boulders, occasional slung horns) interspersed with 3rd/4th-class downclimbing, dropping back onto the Quien Sabe Glacier and the walk back to camp. Loose rock in this gully is a real hazard, and this is where a well-documented, fatal accident occurred on July 10, 2005 (a party that had mistakenly entered this gully was retreating when a natural boulder anchor gave way about 10 feet into the rappel, sending three climbers and the boulder roughly 300 ft down the gully and killing them), so back up questionable anchors, rappel one at a time where the gully is confined, and don't over-trust a single boulder or flake. In July the last rappel down the gully wall is about 30 m and lands at a moat, so a doubled 60 m rope helps clear it.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses.
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier during the approach.
A 2005 anchor-failure accident (a dislodged boulder) killed three climbers on Sharkfin Tower, underscoring the need for solid anchor-building anywhere on the peak.
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food storage canisters are required.

waysIn.name: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, the same window as the Southeast Ridge; being steeper rock it sheds snow a little faster after an early-season storm
waysIn.notes:
Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small unsigned Boston Basin pulloff near 3,200-3,300 ft. The old mining road runs about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, then an unmaintained but well-travelled boot path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams — top off bottles there — to treeline around 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on the knoll above the green meadows at 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully below the tower. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left give an alternate entry and rejoin the couloir about 100 ft up.

There is no separate approach to the Southeast Face. You reach it by climbing the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and rappelling.
hazards: Getting into the wrong gully: on 10 July 2005 a six-person party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here, a climber was struck by rockfall during the roped traverse back toward the standard line, and minutes later a natural boulder anchor failed during the retreat rappel, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth
Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier
The two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains and no rap rings, and there is no anchor at all at the very base of pitch 1
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food canisters required

name: West Ridge (Beckey Route)
approach: From the Depot Creek trailhead parking on the abandoned logging spur off Chilliwack Lake Road (BC) at roughly 2,350 ft, hike the old roadway grade uphill (left-hand fork) for about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk. From there the route follows the unmaintained, unmarked 'Depot Creek climbers path' — a boot-track through old-growth forest for roughly 3 miles that gains to the base of Depot Creek Falls (about 4.8 hours and 1,600 ft in from the cars). The falls are one of the tallest in Washington (drop cited around 900-1,000 ft), and the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along its left edge; a fixed handline is present at the crux scramble section here and this is the approach's main technical hazard (exposed, greasy rock, worse in the wet or in the dark — several parties report losing the tread here at night). Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain, reaching treeline where climbers typically switch to mountaineering boots/crampons. Continue up class 3 tread gaining roughly 800 ft into the Redoubt Glacier basin; Ouzel Lake, in this basin, is the most common first camp. From Ouzel Lake most parties relocate camp 3-4 hours further up onto the Redoubt Glacier saddle/col (~7,150 ft) for a high camp closer to the peaks — this leg is flat glacier travel with only minor, usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions. From high camp, traverse roughly 2 miles east across snow/glacier beneath Easy Mox's south side toward the 'Col of the Wild,' the saddle between Easy and Hard (Southeast) Mox, finishing with a steep ~1,000 ft climb over notoriously unstable, sandy talus (loose rock is the dominant hazard on this whole upper approach — helmets on well before the col). From the Col of the Wild, ascend a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully, then scramble up and right (class 4, exposed enough that many parties belay it) toward a notch in the 'Ridge of Gendarmes.' A short sequence of ledges zig-zagging right-left-right leads through the notch; descend briefly to a small flat area and locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge, which is the start of the roped climbing (two pitches of 5th class to the summit tower, then a final short, exposed class 3 scramble — stay roped — to the true summit). Water is available from the glacier/snowmelt and Ouzel Lake but not reliably along the upper ridge, so carry enough from camp.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent walk-off. From the true summit, most parties make three single-rope (30 m) rappels down the tower to a small, exposed high notch, then one longer double-rope (60 m) rappel from that notch down into the gully/glacier below — roughly four rappels in typical late-summer, snow-free conditions. Anchors along this line are almost entirely improvised rather than bolted: slung boulders, horns and pedestals wrapped with tat/cord, and the occasional jammed knot in a crack; a couple of the stations have accumulated enough old cord to look semi-permanent, but none should be trusted blindly and back-up/extend as needed. Bring a single 60 m rope (or two ropes if you want to do the notch-to-glacier drop as one clean pull rather than downclimbing part of it). In seasons or conditions where a snow finger lingers in the descent gully, parties have needed far more — up to 9-10 shorter single-rope rappels interspersed with downclimbing to get through the same 400-ft gully system, because a lingering snow patch prevents a clean full-length pull; budget extra time and a plan B if you find snow still choking the gully. Known hazards on this descent: persistently loose, choss-prone rock (the Southeast Spire's rock quality is poor, and at least one incident involved a slab breaking loose during rope retrieval at the notch and striking a climber), ropes getting stuck when pulled through the loose gully, high exposure along the east ledges near the Ridge of Gendarmes, and fatigue/darkness on the lower-angle terrain given how long this climb runs. After reaching the glacier below the Col of the Wild, reverse the approach traverse back to your high camp (Redoubt Col/Ouzel Lake), then descend the Depot Creek climbers path past the falls — using the fixed handline again on the steep slab section — back to the trailhead.
hazards: Pervasively loose, rotten gneiss along the entire route — rockfall is the primary objective hazard
Redoubt Glacier crevasses open up as the season progresses — real glacier travel/crevasse-rescue gear is needed, not just a rope for show
Complex route-finding through the gendarmes and gully system on rotten rock — easy to get off-route
Extreme remoteness: multi-day approach on both the US and Canadian sides means any rescue or evacuation takes a long time

waysIn.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
waysIn.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
waysIn.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp

waysIn.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
waysIn.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
waysIn.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the glacier is in good shape and the weather is settled, a party moves up to the saddle camp for a much shorter summit day instead of staying at the lake.

name: Southeast Ridge (SE Corner)
approach: East-northeast up Shannon Ridge, then traverse Sulphide Glacier to reach southeast ridge base By mid-August one stretch of the forest road to the Shannon Ridge trailhead is washed out and high clearance helps; the trail up the ridge is cleared and easy to follow, and the glacier's lowest slope is hard ice at dawn after a cold night, with crevasses right away and no set bootpack. In mid-June the snow is continuous from about 4,700 ft and the basin camp near 6,200 ft has running water and dry pads; slopes above camp can shed wet avalanches onto the trail on the way out.
descent: Rappel the same 4th-class gully used as the standard ascent line up the summit pyramid (the line shared with the Fisher Chimneys/Sulphide Glacier finish); a 60m rope reaches all belay stations.
hazards: Descent rappel traverses a gully that can drop rock onto parties below.
Crevasses on the Sulphide Glacier approach; conditions worsen late in the season.

waysIn.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
waysIn.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.
hazards: Featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft is genuinely hard to navigate in reduced visibility
Crevasses on the Sulphide Glacier, small but present, increasingly open late season
Active rockfall near the bootpack around 5,400 ft, worse in the afternoon; go early
Bergschrund crossing on the upper Sulphide that gets trickier as the glacier opens
Limited protection on sparsely protectable 5.3 rock; severe exposure on both sides of the crest
Descent rappels a gully shared with the standard route; parties above are a rockfall source
Blue ice August-September; sun-softened snow bridges in the afternoon

waysIn.name: Lake Ann and the Fisher Chimneys to the summit pyramid
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR 542, follow the whole Fisher Chimneys route to the foot of the summit pyramid: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the saddle, the climbers' path east to the chimneys, about 1,000 ft of class 3–4 scrambling through them, Winnie's Slide onto the Upper Curtis Glacier, then Hell's Highway onto the upper Sulphide Glacier.

Longer, steeper and more technical than the Shannon Ridge approach, and most parties take two or three days, camping at Lake Ann or above the chimneys. Where the Fisher Chimneys route finishes up the central gully, this one trends right off the glacier and takes the southeast ridge instead.
hazards: Rockfall inside the Fisher Chimneys (about 1,000 ft of class 3-4), especially with parties above
Steep snow or ice on Winnie's Slide, firm before the sun reaches it
Crevasses on the Upper Curtis Glacier
Hell's Highway crosses exposed slopes below the Upper Curtis icefall
Limited protection on sparsely protectable 5.3 rock; severe exposure on both sides of the crest
Descent rappels a gully shared with the standard route; parties above are a rockfall source
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want to camp at Lake Ann or above the chimneys on a multi-day trip and accept scrambling with rockfall risk; longer and more technical than Shannon Ridge.

name: Southwest Buttress
approach: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. Where the Southwest Buttress approach diverges is the final glacier traverse: from camp, continue across the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister Glacier, heading toward the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The base of the Southwest Buttress is reached via a prominent gully - often snow-filled year-round - that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
descent: From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to a large rock/boulder on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, where a fixed rappel ring and sling (recently reported as reinforced with an additional sling) anchors the route's single rappel: a double-rope rappel (both strands, ~60m rope) that lowers you to a steep snow slope which, in normal-season conditions, keeps a solid connection to the rock, so a moat crossing usually isn't required at this point. From the bottom of that rappel, downclimb/glissade the snow slope to the notch at the base of the route - the same notch used on the approach - and reverse the glacier travel back toward camp. Some parties describe an alternate single-rope-length rappel off the top of the summit gully instead of the ridge-boulder station; functionally this is still a one-rappel descent, just from a slightly different anchor. Either way, plan on exactly one rope-length transition, not a multi-pitch rappel sequence - the rest of the descent is downclimbing, scrambling, and glacier travel. Because this is a moderate Grade III+ route rather than a big-wall-style descent, no v-thread or chained-rappel sequence is needed in summer conditions; the main descent hazard is the moat at the base of the route staying open or widening late in the season, which can complicate reconnecting with the glacier.
hazards: steep, often snow-filled approach gully (to about 35°)
exposed knife-edge summit ridge
crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration/McAllister Glaciers en route

waysIn.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
waysIn.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
waysIn.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top

name: South Ridge ("Spirited Away")
approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. From the pass, stay on the maintained trail as it drops past Boundary Camp and Copper Creek Camp into the Chilliwack valley; roughly two miles beyond Copper Creek an easily missed side path leads down to the Chilliwack River ford (about 2,750 ft), and the Easy Ridge path climbs steeply from the far bank. From here it is sustained, largely cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned it becomes brutal later in the season and in dry years. Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.
descent: The descent does not reverse the ridge. Both of the route's rappels — about 25 m into the gap at the Pitch 7 gendarme and about 30 m off the final hoodoo tower — are made on the way up, below the last ~600 ft of scrambling to the top, so a single 60 m rope covers them. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. From the summit, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, relaxed steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the usual endless scree and loose talus that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.
hazards: Loose, exfoliating 'choss' rock through the upper hoodoo section, with isolated runout 5.9 moves on suspect rock
Glaciated, route-finding-intensive approach via Challenger Col/Challenger Glacier vicinity — crevasse hazard
Multi-day commitment far from any road, trail, or cell coverage; slow self-rescue/evacuation
Only two documented ascents (2006, 2022) — minimal current-conditions beta

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Challenger Col
waysIn.season: Midsummer to early autumn; Easy Ridge is hot, dry and shadeless and would be brutal late in the season or in a dry year, so time it for when water is still running on the crest
waysIn.notes: This is one of the longest approaches in the range and takes two or more travel days each way. From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead follow the maintained trail to the pass, then descend the far side into the Chilliwack valley, past the Copper Ridge branch, to the river ford below Easy Ridge — that low point is the bottom of the whole trip. Switchback back up onto Easy Ridge and follow the open, dry crest over Easy Peak to the bivy beyond it. Day two crosses the Imperfect Impasse, regains Challenger Col, and traverses the southern Challenger cirque to the west ridge of Phantom Peak, the usual second camp. From there it is cross-country across the western slopes to the foot of the ridge.
hazards: Cold, thigh-deep Chilliwack ford in early season — cross before the afternoon melt
A bergschrund opens near the top of Challenger Col by mid to late season
The Imperfect Impasse must be downclimbed and re-ascended and is consistently slower than it looks
Sustained loose and shattered rock on the ridge, including a gendarme that needs a rappel into the gap

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FS Road 4065), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (#707) into the Morning Star NRCA. About 0.5 mile in, the trail makes a tricky crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish River — no bridge, sometimes aided by a small-diameter log and a hand rope; this ford can be genuinely difficult and dangerous after heavy rain or early-season snowmelt. Beyond the crossing the trail climbs gradually through forest for roughly a mile to Wirtz Basin, where the terrain opens up and turns rockier. From the basin the trail steepens sharply into a narrow, loose rock chute switchbacking up to Headlee Pass (4,720 ft, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead) — this chute is notorious for rockfall dislodged by parties above and is also an avalanche path in shoulder-season/spring snow conditions, so groups should spread out and move through it deliberately. From Headlee Pass the trail contours around Sperry's south/east flank and drops slightly into the upper Vesper Creek basin to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, roughly 3 miles in). Leave the maintained trail at the lake's outlet, follow its east shore, then climb open, welcoming slopes to the saddle/notch between Vesper and Sperry Peaks (Sperry Saddle). From the saddle it's off-trail scrambling up Sperry's west ridge/west slope — loose, often wet dirt and heather with class 3 rock steps, including some brushy, tree-assisted moves in the final push to the summit block — to the 6,120 ft summit. Total distance to the top is around 4 miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain; water is available at the South Fork crossing and at Vesper Lake but not much beyond it, so top off before leaving the lake.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose, brushy west ridge/west slope scramble back to Sperry Saddle, then drop to the Vesper Lake outlet and rejoin the maintained Sunrise Mine Trail. Route-finding on the upper scramble is the main hazard on the way down — the easiest line up is not obvious from above, and it's easy to end up descending a different, steeper gully than the one you climbed, so note landmarks (the climber's-right ramp and the cairned dirt path into the trees) on the way up and look for them again on the way down. From the lake, retrace the trail back through Headlee Pass and down its rockfall-prone switchback chute (loose underfoot, stay alert for rock knocked loose by other parties), through Wirtz Basin, back across the South Fork Stillaguamish ford, and out to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling involved anywhere on the standard line.
hazards: Difficult, sometimes thigh-deep early-season ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish River at ~0.5 mi from the trailhead
Steep, narrow rock chute below Headlee Pass explicitly flagged by the Forest Service as notorious for falling rocks, especially with other parties above
Eroded switchbacks to Headlee Pass exceeding 50 degrees in places, awkward with a pack and worse on tired legs during descent
Loose rock and confusing routefinding on the upper Class 3 scramble — easy to end up off-route in brush or cliffed above steeper terrain than intended
Lingering snow into midsummer on shaded aspects; ice axe/crampons often still needed into July in the Headlee Pass gully

waysIn.name: Headlee Pass and Lake Elan
waysIn.season: July to early October, once the Headlee Pass chute is clear of snow
waysIn.notes: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead the trail makes an awkward, sometimes roped crossing of the South Fork about half a mile in, climbs through forest to Wirtz Basin, then steepens sharply into a narrow, loose chute switchbacking to Headlee Pass. Beyond the pass the trail contours the peak's south and east flank and drops into the upper basin at Lake Elan. Leave the maintained trail at the lake outlet. Water is available at the river crossing and the lake and essentially nowhere above it, so fill before leaving.
hazards: The South Fork crossing can be dangerous after heavy rain or in early-season melt
The Headlee Pass chute is notorious for rockfall from parties above and is an avalanche path in shoulder-season snow
Loose, often wet dirt and heather with class 3 steps on the upper third of the peak

name: South Slopes Scramble
approach: Park at the Yodelin lot on US 2 (the former Yodelin ski area's lot, now used for overflow parking, roughly 1.7 miles from the Stevens Pass Ski Area pedestrian overpass, around milepost 60). Cross the highway and follow the old ski-area road to its end, then head west up the valley, staying near Nason Creek where crossings/snow bridges are most reliable, then continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye Peak ridge before turning up to the gap below Point 5261.
descent: Reverse the ascent line back through the gap and down into the basin to the Nason Creek valley and the Yodelin lot. With a stable, consolidated snowpack the open basin can offer a quick glissade or snowshoe/ski descent, but avoid dropping onto the Pacific Crest Trail tread itself for winter travel — it crosses several avalanche paths near here.
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the approach basin and along nearby Pacific Crest Trail chutes — check NWAC Stevens Pass zone forecast
Narrow, corniced ridge beyond Point 5261 on the more direct variant — exposed, requires an ice axe
No maintained trail — off-trail route-finding through timber and open basin, with little to no boot-packed track most of the season
Thick brush/devil's club bushwhacking if attempted after snowmelt

waysIn.name: Nason Creek basin to the Point 5261 col
waysIn.season: January to May, on snowpack
waysIn.notes: Park in the overflow lot off US-2 a couple of miles east of the ski area, cross the highway on foot and pick up the old ski-area access road into the valley, keeping near the creek where crossings and snow bridges are most reliable. Continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye ridge before turning up toward the gap. Almost every ascent is made on winter or spring snowpack; once the snow is gone this is a thick, unpleasant bushwhack that parties generally avoid, so the season is short and conditions-driven rather than weather-driven.
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the approach basin and in the nearby chutes
A narrow, corniced connecting ridge on the harder variant
No maintained trail and rarely a boot-packed track
Thick devil's club and brush once the snow melts out
Windblown snow that ices the sub-summit ridge

name: Standard Route
approach: Drive US-2 to Skykomish, then north on Beckler River Road (FR-65) for about 15 miles; turn left (west) onto FR-63 and follow it about 4.6 miles to where it crosses the North Fork Skykomish River again. Just past that bridge the road bends right over a small rise about a mile east of Galena (~1,150 ft); park at the unmarked roadside pullout there. Leave the road on the side away from the river and head directly, off-trail, up the steep, blowdown-choked slope toward Spire Mountain. There is no tread anywhere on the mountain: the line works around cliff bands at roughly 4,200-4,400 ft on the peak's north side, traverses southeast to about 5,400 ft below the summit spires, and gains the west/northwest ridge for the final scramble to the top. An older, historic alternate approach (Fred Beckey's original line) starts south of Index via the North Fork Skykomish River Road, which now dead-ends at a washout around mile 6, then follows the unmaintained Trout Creek Road south to reach the same ridge — a much brushier ~16-mile, ~7,000 ft round trip, longer than today's standard FR-63 approach. Straight off the parking pullout the first stretch is thick fern hiding deadfall, which is slow in the dark in July; after the first old logging road the going is easier.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb (or rappel/back off facing in) the short Class 5 step near 6,100 ft, then retrace the ridge and the off-trail descent back through the 5,400 ft traverse and the 4,200-4,400 ft cliff-band bypass back down to the FR-63 roadside pullout. Loose rock, brush, and the lack of a defined tread make the descent slow going — budget real time for it and avoid straying north or east into steeper terrain where permanent snow/ice and cliffs persist.
hazards: Steep, entirely off-trail approach through blowdown and brush, especially the first ~600 ft above the river
Cliff bands around 4,200-4,400 ft on the peak's north side that require careful route-finding to bypass
Exposed ~10 ft Class 5 mantle step at roughly 6,100 ft on the summit ridge — a clear step up from the Class 3 ridge around it
Permanent ice/snow patches on north and east aspects near the summit, present even in late summer
North Fork Skykomish River crossing can be hazardous during high water or early-season snowmelt
No reliable cell coverage anywhere on route

waysIn.name: North Fork Skykomish riverside to the northwest saddle
waysIn.season: Late July to September
waysIn.notes: Everything above the valley is off-trail. Leave the riverside near the road and head directly up the steep, blowdown-choked slope — the first several hundred feet are the worst of it — onto a well-defined hogsback that runs from about 2,700 ft to roughly 3,300 ft. Above the hogsback the slope steepens toward cliff bands, and there is no tread anywhere on the mountain. Carry water from the river; there is none once you leave it, and there is no usable cell coverage anywhere on route.
hazards: Entirely off-trail with sustained blowdown and brush low down
Cliff bands on the north side between roughly 4,200 and 4,400 ft that need careful route-finding to turn
A moat or bergschrund forming at the saddle depending on snow cover
Permanent snow and ice on north and east aspects near the summit even in late summer
A short exposed class 5 step considerably harder than the route's overall grade suggests

name: Southeast Face
approach: Start at the Downey Creek Trailhead (end of FR 26/Suiattle River Road, elev. ~1,450'). Follow the Downey Creek Trail (#792) roughly 6.5 miles of gentle, well-graded old-growth forest walking — recent Forest Service work has added boardwalks and new log bridges — to Sixmile Camp and the final log crossing of Bachelor Creek at about 2,400'. From the north side of that crossing, pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path: it starts as a distinct boot-track climbing steeply beside the creek, then eases into switchbacks. Expect brushy, overgrown sections (salmon berry and vine maple) through the 4,000' meadows; the path fords Bachelor Creek again near a campsite, then climbs an avalanche chute on switchbacks before ducking back into trees on climber's left. Around 5,900' the path tops out on the forested ridge above Cub Lake — descend ~500' on steep switchbacks to the lake (good camping), skirt its north shore, and continue to Itswoot Ridge, where a stream draining the Spire Point basin gives a reliable camp/water source at roughly 6,400'. This is the natural high camp for the route (car-to-camp is already ~12-13 miles and 5,000'+ of gain). From camp, hike north up Itswoot Ridge staying on talus on its west (left) side near the stream to bypass rock towers directly above camp; the ridge crest itself is only walkable in short gentle sections. You'll hit permanent snow before Spire Col (7,760'): either climb moderate ~30° snow straight up to the col, or skirt around the left edge of the snowfield on rock. From the col, contour/climb east on talus and broken ledges roughly 400-500' to the base of the southwest face, where the route starts up loose talus into a short (~30') Class 4 chimney. Rope up for the exposed Class 4-5.5 face/chimney climbing above. Hazards: creek fords on Bachelor Creek can be swift in early season, the Bachelor Creek path is brushy and easy to lose, the avalanche chute holds snow late and is exposed to slide activity into early summer, and the final approach to the col crosses glacier-remnant snow that firms up icy in morning — an axe and possibly crampons are standard kit into midsummer.
descent: Descend the same southwest face line rather than a separate walk-off. From the tiny, exposed summit horn, parties typically belay the last person down/back from the highest ledge (3rd ledge below the true summit) using slings around the horn as an anchor, then set up rappels from that ledge system rather than the summit itself for more working room. The standard sequence is two rappels of roughly 28-30 meters each — done with a single 60m rope doubled (not two full 60m raps) — down natural sling/webbing anchors (no bolts reported): the first rappel drops to an anchor just above the Class 4 chimney passed on the way up, and the second rappel from there reaches easy talus at the base of the chimney/face. From there, downclimb and reverse the talus/ledges back to Spire Col, then retrace the approach: down the snow/talus to Itswoot Ridge, around Cub Lake, down the Bachelor Creek path, and out the Downey Creek Trail. Watch for loose rock in the chimney and on the ledges (this is broken alpine granite, not a clean crack system), confirm sling anchors are sound/not sun-bleached before weighting them, and back up questionable webbing with your own if in doubt. Because the approach and descent share the same brushy, routefinding-heavy Bachelor Creek path, budget real time and daylight for the reversal — parties commonly camp at Itswoot Ridge or Cub Lake both nights rather than pushing the whole thing car-to-car.
hazards: Loose, fractured rock in the class 4 chimney and ledge sections
Extreme exposure (1,000+ ft) on the ledges above the Spire Glacier
Afternoon thunderstorms/lightning, common in July-August
Crevasses/moats on the Spire and Dana Glacier margins in early season
Very long, remote approach with slow potential rescue response

waysIn.name: Bachelor Creek, Itswoot Ridge and Spire Col
waysIn.season: Midsummer to early autumn; snow is usually continuous above about 6,800 ft and firms up icy in the morning
waysIn.notes: From the Downey Creek Trailhead follow the well-graded valley trail through old-growth to Sixmile Camp and the log crossing of Bachelor Creek. From the north side pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path: a distinct boot-track beside the creek at first, then switchbacks, then salmonberry and vine maple through the meadows around 4,000 ft. It fords the creek again near a campsite, climbs an avalanche chute, and tops out on the forested ridge above Cub Lake. Drop to the lake, skirt its north shore, and regain the crest to the Itswoot Ridge camp with its stream from the basin above. From camp, hike north up the ridge staying on talus on its west side to bypass the towers directly overhead, then take moderate snow or the rock at the snowfield's left edge to the col.
hazards: The Bachelor Creek path is brushy, overgrown and easy to lose — the route-finding crux of the approach
The avalanche chute holds snow late and is exposed to slide activity into early summer
Loose talus and kicked-down rock in the summit chimney
The summit horn holds one climber at a time above well over a thousand feet of air

name: Spontaneity Arete
approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line. In mid-June a patch of avalanche debris lies across the path, and the steeper climbers' trail above has three fixed hand-lines.
descent: Most parties rappel the line of the route, which some report takes a long time (about 9 rappels, with occasional rope snags on flakes requiring re-ascent to free them). The alternative is descending the 3rd-class gully climber's right of the route, which is faster but described as loose and 'gnarly' — staying high and skier's-right reduces exposure to looseness. From the summit anchor drop into the gully on the descent-right side, then walk its loose floor, staying right first and left once it narrows.
hazards: Documented accident (2018): climbers started about 10 ft off-route and built an unanchored belay during the downclimb; a 15 ft factor fall onto a 30° dirt slope resulted in a broken wrist and helicopter evacuation.

waysIn.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, the fixed-rope climbers' trail
waysIn.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and the approach snowfield have melted out
waysIn.notes:
Drive east over Washington Pass and park in the turnout about two miles beyond it, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. This is a highway pullout, not a trailhead — nothing is signed.

The climbers' path leaves the west or south-west end of the turnout and drops steeply through loose dirt and rock into the trees. It is well worn but unmarked apart from intermittent cairns. It crosses Early Winters Creek on logs and resumes on the far side, then climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation.

Higher up the old line uses two or three fixed lines on an avalanche path before topping out on a flat area. A newer variation bears right just before the fixed lines are reached and needs only a small amount of scrambling; most parties now prefer it. Reckon roughly an hour and a half.

Do not treat the fixed ropes as maintained equipment. They are informal, weathered, and nobody replaces them on a schedule.
hazards: Weathered informal fixed ropes on the old approach line; the newer right-bearing variation avoids them
Early Winters Creek is crossed on logs and is worse in high water
Long unroped scrambling between pitches on a route people rack up for as a 5.7
Rappelling the line is slow and ropes snag on flakes, sometimes needing re-ascent to free them
The alternative descent gully is loose and sits above the approach path

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Trailhead is the West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trailhead (Trail #411), reached via Twisp River Road ~10.7-10.8 miles from Twisp, then left on Buttermilk Creek Road, staying left onto East Buttermilk Road (Forest Road 43) for roughly 4 miles, then right onto the Road 500 spur for about 2.7 miles to the road-end trailhead at about 3,960 ft. From there Trail #411 climbs the West Fork Buttermilk Creek drainage into the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Tread is inconsistently maintained in the lower-to-mid section — parties describe long stretches of blowdown with only brief clear tread, so plan to navigate by map/GPS rather than blazes. Several fords of the West Fork are the main early-season hazard: in June/early summer with high runoff these crossings can be genuinely difficult, sometimes requiring a detour upstream to find a log crossing. About 2 miles before Star Lake the trail enters the lowest larches, and roughly a half mile before the lake it crests Fish Creek Pass, an open viewpoint over the larch-covered Sawtooth Range and a good landmark/rest stop with reliable water nearby. From the pass, the trail drops about 300 ft into the Star Lake basin (~7,180 ft) — 7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of gain from the trailhead. Snow commonly lingers on the upper approach slopes into summer (encountered from roughly 6,000 ft up in early-season conditions), so a light axe/spikes are worth carrying outside of late-season. From Star Lake, pick up a climber's trail heading up into the bowl south of the lake, contour around Point 7912, and gain the SW ridge; a steep, loose scree track leads from the basin up to the ridge crest. From there it's scree-walking, talus-hopping, and some easy Class 2-3 hands-and-feet scrambling along the ridge east to the 8,693 ft summit. Total one-way distance from trailhead to summit runs roughly 8.5-9 miles with about 4,730 ft of cumulative gain. An alternate approach uses the Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan to Prince Creek Landing, then climbs North Fork Prince Creek to the Sawtooth crest and reaches Star Peak via Star Pass — the classic way to combine it with Courtney Peak and other Sawtooth summits.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling on the standard Southwest Ridge scramble route. From the summit, reverse the ridge scramble back down to the head of the scree slope, then descend the same loose scree/talus line back into the Star Lake basin. Stay on or near the ascent line: do not descend the boulder field on the east side of the peak, which is dangerous with unstable, car-sized talus. Loose rock and scree underfoot make the descent slow and slippery regardless of line, and if snow is still present on the upper slopes it typically softens through the day, so rock underneath can pull loose late — an earlier start/turnaround reduces this. From Star Lake, reverse the West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trail (#411): back up over Fish Creek Pass, down through the larch zone, through the blowdown-choked lower trail, and back across the West Fork Buttermilk Creek fords to the trailhead.
hazards: Loose, unstable talus and scree, described in trip reports as 'massively unstable' at the base of the summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning exposure on the open SW ridge and summit
Off-trail route-finding above Star Lake, including a tricky contour around Point 7,912
Long, remote approach (7.5+ miles one-way) with minimal-to-no cell coverage

waysIn.name: West Fork Buttermilk to Star Lake
waysIn.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
waysIn.notes: Seven and a half miles of trail from the West Fork Buttermilk road end to Star Lake, and the tread is inconsistently maintained through the middle of it — long stretches of blowdown with only brief clear sections, so navigate by map or track rather than by looking for tread. Several fords of the West Fork are the main early-season problem and can force a detour upstream to find a log. Two miles below the lake the trail enters the lowest larches, and half a mile before it the trail crests Fish Creek Pass, an open viewpoint with water nearby and the first clear look at the peak. The lake basin is the standard camp and also serves several neighbouring summits. A boat-in approach from Lake Chelan up Prince Creek reaches the same crest from the other side.
hazards: Large, deeply unstable talus at the base of the summit block
Rockfall onto anyone below on the loose scree track, worst on descent
Off-trail route-finding above the lake, including a contour that is easy to lose in snow
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on a wholly open ridge
High fords early in the season
Long and remote with minimal cell coverage

name: North Face
approach: Approach from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley (North Bend side): drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (NF-56) to its plowed/drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance (about 1 mile in the FA party's case) into the valley. Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing multiple braids of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River (the crux of the approach in high water), then climb to a camp below the north face. The FA party's full approach from vehicle to camp took about 6.5 hours.
descent: From the summit area, downclimb neve on the southwest aspect to the top of a snow gully, then make two 30m rappels down the gully to regain lower-angle terrain and return toward the approach basin/camp.
hazards: A non-standard, rarely-climbed alpine ice route with almost no repeat trip-report beta
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on the spring approach and snowfields

waysIn.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley in spring, river braids and a camp below the face
waysIn.season: A narrow spring window, roughly March to April, while the ice and snowfields are in. This line forms only briefly and has almost no repeat trip-report history
waysIn.notes:
Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road, NF-56, to its plowed or drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance — about a mile in the first-ascent party's case — into the valley.

Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing multiple braids of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie. Those crossings are the crux of the approach in high water and are unprotected. Then climb to a camp below the north face. The first-ascent party took about six and a half hours from vehicle to camp.
hazards: A rarely-climbed alpine ice route with essentially no repeat beta
Difficult, unprotected crossings of multiple river braids on the approach
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on the spring approach and the snowfields
Near-constant spindrift funnelling down the runnels during and after storm; spindrift avalanches swept the face during the first ascent party's descent
Scarce rock protection between ice sections
A descent by an unfamiliar side of the peak at the end of a committing route
